utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. You may begin, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning, Mr. President. Your Honour, one short matter, and it is all right if the witness is here before I commence. This witness is a serving officer in the Dutch Armed Forces and like the officer that we had here a few weeks ago has been brought to the Tribunal from active service in of an Afghanistan. I have 45 minutes on direct. I do not anticipate using all of this. And I have told the Dutch army, which is quite concerned about scheduling, that I believe that the witness will be free to go at 1.00 this afternoon or earlier, and I just say that for the information of those present. Sir, could you please begin by--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please bear in mind, that while we will try to accommodate the witness, the business of the court takes precedence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I never doubted that, Mr. President, but I also didn't want to put that on the record at quarter to 1.00, which I think would be not desirable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Sir, could you please begin by introducing yourself, tell us your name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: I'm Ronald Eimers, I'm a Dutch citizen, and I was born on December 20th, 1961.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: I'm an officer in the Dutch army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: How long have you been in the Dutch army?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Since March 1983.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And in the Dutch army, what rank do you currently hold?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: I'm an infantry major.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What is your current assignment with the Dutch army?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: I'm the OPs officer with an armoured infantry battalion deployed in Afghanistan right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Major Eimers, on the 10th of November, 1995, did you meet with people from this Tribunal and give a statement.

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yeah. That was the first time I was asked to reveal any information about my period serving as an UNMO in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And on the 13th of October of 2006, did you meet again with people from the Tribunal and give a statement?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Since you came to the Hague the day before yesterday, have you had a chance to review those statements in the English language?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And when you did that, did you find that those written records of the statement accurately showed what you had said on those two occasions?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If we were to ask the same questions that the investigators asked, today, would we get the same answers that you gave on those two-- on those two earlier dates?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time, I tender those two statements. The one from 1995 has 65 ter number 3112. The one from 2006 has 65 ter number 3113.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We admit them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 03112 becomes Exhibit P584. 65 ter number 03113 becomes P585.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Major, in answering a question a couple of manipulates ago, you made reference to being an UNMO in Sarajevo. Can you tell the Court what month and date you began your UNMO Sarajevo in -- I'm sorry, month and year, and what month and year you ended your UNMO service in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: I started in October 1994 until April 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: During your time in Sarajevo, what part of the Sarajevo area were you stationed in?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: For the first week, I was stationed in an UNMO team in Vogosca in the north of Sarajevo; and the rest of my period, I was staged in Hrasnica, which is in the south of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And just for refreshing memory, Hrasnica is that area sort of sandwiched between the airport and Mount Igman; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. Major, during the time that you were in Sarajevo and, specifically, during the time that you were in Hrasnica, could you tell us in two or three sentences what your duties were. What was your job? Why were you there?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: In the first couple of weeks, I served as a team member. Later on, I became the team leader. The tasks that we were to fulfil was to observe what was going on in that area from the military perspective, so what was going on between both warring factions where the front lines were, and actually had an all the actions were from the military point of view. And, secondly, to monitor what was going on on the civil side, say, the humanitarian aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. So the second part, would that be more certain with civilians?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to switch topics a bit here, Major, with my next question. During your career in the Dutch armies infantry, have you had the occasion to command units that have mortars within them?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, briefly, what that experience consists of?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: For two years, have I been a company commander; and, in my company, I had a mortar squad which I directly commanded and I was responsible for its training and its operational deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. And at other times in your career, even if you are not commanding mortars, have you had occasion as an infantry officer to use mortars or to interact with mortar crews?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: I have up till now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And based on that experience, are you able to tell by observing a mortar crew whether they are good at what they are doing?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. And you chuckle when you say that. Why is that?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Well, the fact is that we are deploying mortars right now in Afghanistan, and I'm currently working with them on a day-to-day basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. While in you were in Hrasnica, did you have opportunity to observe the work of mortar crews within the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yes, especially during my first week when I was deployed in Vogosca. We, on a day-to-day basis, met the crews that were in the hills north of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And based on that experience, was that enough of an opportunity for you to form an opinion as to how good these crews were as -- as mortar crews?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Officially, they were, at that time, only there to do maintenance to the mortar pieces and the artillery pieces that were officially in the, how do you call it, Weapons Collection Point. But, like I said, we talked to them on a day-to-day basis, and we, yes, could have a fair opinion about their skills and drills.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Later on, in Hrasnica, did you observe mortar fire when it fell, that was fired from Sarajevo-Romanija Corps mortars?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Well, we never actually observed falling of the grenades, but we did observe the results of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And based -- would observing those results give you a basis for drawing any conclusions about the quality of the mortar crews who had fired those grenades?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: When I look back on the context in which the fire actually was fired, I'm pretty sure that they were always pretty accurate and they must have known what they were targeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, I want to elaborate on a couple of points in your second statement, the one from 2006, and specifically I'm going to go through paragraphs 36 and 37. In paragraph 36, you make reference to UNMOs occasionally needing to arrange cease-fires. Do you know what I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Can you give the Court some examples or a description, whatever is easiest for you to explain, when it was that an UNMO would need a cease-fire in order to carry out that UNMO's job?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Well, there were several occasions in which civilians got hurt during military exchange of fire, occasions in which there were casualties, and we saw it fit and our duties to relieve them from the areas that they were at that moment in and get them to safety; or at moments when actually UNMOs were in danger and we tried to get a situation in which we could get out the cross-fires.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. Did you yourself personally ever have to arrange one of these short cease-fires?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Definitely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And did you speak to colleagues of yours who had also had to arrange these short cease-fires?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yes. That was pretty easy, because there was one operational radio net for all UNMOs in Sarajevo. So whenever a situation like that occurred, every UNMO in the area in the vicinity of a radio would listen in and hear what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. Based on that, can you tell the Court what procedure would UNMOs follow if they needed to have a cease-fire for half an hour, 20 minutes, what have you. In order to get some civilians out or in order to get themselves out, what would they do?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: First of all, we would call in to our OPs officer in the PTT building and, secondly, we would call into the guy called Lima, which was the LO on the BSA side and actually lived in Lukavica Barracks, or to what we referred as Papa. He was the LO on the Bosniak side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: They would do their business then inside the HQs, and we would get confirmation that the fire would be stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned this person Lima, and I take it that's not the real name. That as the radio call sign?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: That's the call sign of the guy, because the UNMOs in Lukavica HQ shifted, of course, as well. Most of the time there were two, and their call sign was Lima.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And was Lima always in Lukavica Barracks?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: No, it was not. They had to do their administrative patrols, they had to bring in their reports to PTT building, et cetera, but, basically, their station was Lukavica Barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And you mentioned a moment ago they actually had their accommodation in Lukavica Barracks?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: When you or your colleagues called Lima, if the request was agreed to, do you have an estimate of typically how long it took before fire ceased?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Especially when the LOs were inside Lukavica Barracks, it would take about five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And during the time that you were an UNMO in Sarajevo, was there an opportunity for you to see the kind of communication equipment that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: No. I have never personally witnessed the actual equipment they used, but I was told by the guys called Lima that they had very modern equipment to scan our radios. So the actual radio message from us wasn't that necessary and the action of Lima never was that necessary, because they knew what we were radioing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If I could jump in at this point with a follow-up question. Did Lima describe to you the equipment was used for Lukavica to communicate with Sarajevo-Romanija Corps units in the field around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court what Lima told you about Sarajevo-Romanija Corps' ability to communicate with units in the field?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: They used radios and telephone land lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: From a military point of view, how sophisticated were the communications within the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps? How advanced?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: I guess it is fair to say that they used the same kind of means that I used in my army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, during the time that you were an UNMO in Hrasnica, did you also have the occasion to meet with small unit commanders within the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: During my stay in Hrasnica, I once had a longer meeting with the brigade commander in Ilidza. It was during the cease-fire period, and he showed us his positions in the east -- sorry, in the west of the Hrasnica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Besides this meeting with the brigade commander during the cease-fire period, were there other occasions when you met with commanders of other small units, maybe on a briefer or a less extended basis but, nonetheless, met with them and talked with them?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: No. The only other time when I met with commanders was in my first week when I was in Vogosca, and the only meeting I then had with one of the commanders was during a funeral. So it was very brief and not about military aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: During any of these conversations, did you talk with small unit commanders, whether it was the brigade commander or one of these other short meetings in Vogosca. Did you have any conversations about how much independent decision-making authority they had?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: No, not that specific. But I was always under the impression that it was a tight chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: When you say you are "always under the impression there was a tight chain of command," what do you base that impression on? What facts did you observe that led you to form that impression?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: The way that the military hierarchy inside their ranks was obvious gave me the impression that they were doing their things in a military perspective that I was very familiar with. So considering the situation that the entire Sarajevo area was not that big, and they had the right means of communication, it was clear to me that they would have a proper chain of command and proper lines of communication, just like I was used to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Just like in the Dutch army?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, were you ever -- during the time that you were travelling around the Sarajevo area, there were a number of checkpoints in the area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yeah. The areas that were not immediately covered by trenches, especially the roads, were always occupied with checkpoints from both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And I want to limit this for now to the checkpoints by the army of Republika Srpska, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Were you ever stopped at those checkpoints or held up at those checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yes, I was on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And did you ever have a conversation with the people manning the checkpoints about whether they had the authority on their own to make the decision whether to stop you or whether to let you proceed about your business?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: We always made conversation obviously because you wanted to get through; but on a number of occasions when we were definitely stopped, we tried to find out why and it was made clear to us that it was because it was ordered so, and especially because they knew that my team was from the Bosniak side. They knew that getting to Mount Igman, especially in the winter, for us it was absolutely needed to cross these checkpoints to use the what was called the Olympic road to get to the higher ground of Mount Igman, which was part of my team's AOR as well. They knew that if we couldn't cross they would stop us and, therefore, limit freedom of movement completely. And on a number of occasions -- occasion, we had this conversations and it was made clear to us that the order came way from the top to stop us, and they would still be freedom of movement for the other team, especially those that were deployed on the Serb side. But for the Bosniak side teams, we would be stopped and sent back.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm going to move on now to paragraph 37 of your second statement, in which you say that it was your opinion that were there no "rogue elements" - those were your words - operating in the Sarajevo area. First of all, do you stand by that statement today?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I have never seen any of those elements operate or even present.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. And, lastly, speaking again of liaison officers, you talked about Lima who was an SRK officer inside Lukavica. Did the UNMOs also have liaison officers inside Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's what I said. The guy called Lima was an UNMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: He had direct contact with liaison officers from the Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I apologise. I think I misunderstood. I thought Lima was the call sign of the SRK liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: It is the UNMO liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And just to be clear, that UNMO liaison officer would then speak to an SRK opposite number?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for the clarification. In that you were both UNMOs, you and people filling the Lima job, did you ever speak with those UNMO liaison officers about conversations they had had inside Lukavica Barracks with officers of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Every now and then, but very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Were there conversations that you had with UNMO liaison officers about things SRK officers had said, regarding level of response they would make to Bosnian attacks or damage inflicted on the Serbian side by Bosnian attacks?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yes. It was made clear to them and, therefore, to the entire UNMO community that whatever attacks would be launched on the Serb side, whether it was military or civilian, would be retaliated at least twice as hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: During your time as an UNMO in Hrasnica and the observations that you made of the situation, was that prediction of that threat in fact carried into action, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: There was a couple of times that we got word that there were Serb civilians killed on one day, and then we could predict the next day we would get mortars incoming in the area where I lived, yes. And that actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, that concludes the direct examination. I have no more questions in chief for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My learned friend Mr. Docherty was very concise, and I will do my best to conclude my cross-examination as soon as possible and that Mr. Eimers will be able to resume his professional duties soon

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Eimers. I appear for Mr. Dragomir Milosevic here as his Defence counsel. My name is Branislav Tapuskovic, Attorney-at-law, and I would like to question about some assertions contained in your statement. I would appreciate it if you could be as precise as possible in your answers and brief in the interests of time, which is always pressing here. First of all, I would like to ask you about the statement you gave on the 13th of October, 2006 because, in a way, it is more precise in explaining the matters you have dealt with in your first statement. But I would also like to go through your first statement, given on the 10th and 11th October, 1995. That's Prosecution Exhibit P584. I would single out some passages in that statement that deal with general matters, and we will go into details in your second statement. You have the statement in front of you, and you can confirm that it indeed reflects your answers to the questions of investigators. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In this first paragraph, if you would be so kind as to confirm, you were a member of the infantry. You did not specialise in mortars at the time.

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: At the time I was in the infantry, yes, and my experience with mortars were limited then as to now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We see here that you said in the former Yugoslavia you were from the 26th October, 1994 until the 26th of April, 1995. Is that correct? Was your last day the 4th of April? It's written in the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: The 4th of April was my last day in Sarajevo, and the 26th of April was the last day in the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking this because the 4th of April is an important moment that the Trial Chamber should learn certain things about, but you were first in Vogosca which falls within the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: That's correct. Like I already said, during the first week, I served in the Vogosca team.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since you spent eight days there, could you explain to the Trial Chamber the geographical position of Vogosca relative to the hills above it? Was it in the foot of Zuc hill in a depression, in a valley?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: The position of the accommodation was in the centre of Vogosca, and the area of operations was limited to the -- to the east to the Blazuj area and -- sorry to the west to the Blazuj area; and to the east, it covered the hillsides over-watching Sarajevo until the -- the area of the television tower. So the area just over Sarajevo, north of Sarajevo, was inside the area of operations of the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Eimers, I'll try to simplify my question. Vogosca was at the foot of mountains, or rather, hills that were under the control of the BH army. It was below Zuc mountain and Hum.

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Well, either I don't get the question correct or, otherwise, I would have to say that the Vogosca area was controlled by the BSA and not by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I was really not clear. I know that Vogosca was under the control of the Bosnian Serb army, but who controlled Zuc hill and was Vogosca at the foot of that hill? Could you confirm that Zuc hill was under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that simply because I don't remember the name Zuc hill, and therefore I cannot point out where it actually is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that you can't remember the name, but was Vogosca at the foot of a hill that was controlled by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Vogosca was at the foot of a hill, and even more south it was controlled by the BH army. But like I said before, I can't point out the actual location that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If it were shown to you on a map, would that help?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why don't you show it to him on a map?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't think that would be necessary because the answer I got from the witness is that Vogosca was indeed at the foot of a hill. He just can't remember the name of the hill, but he confirmed that it was at the foot of a hill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have just a few questions with regard to this statement, as I said. This was page 2 in B/C/S and page 3, paragraph 7 in English. Now we are on page 4 in B/C/S. Do you see the paragraph that begins with the words: "After my arrival at Hrasnica on 8 November." Could you please focus on the third sentence of that paragraph that says: "At the beginning of my stint in Hrasnica, there was not that much shelling." Could you confirm that it was a period in which there were not many of those incidents, militarily speaking?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: In the beginning of my stay in Hrasnica, there was a lot of military activity, but it was not shelling, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at English page 4, and it's page 5 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Second paragraph in the English version says: "As from 20th November 1995, the attack on Bihac started and we were not allowed to go out. So, in that period, we did not conduct any investigations. After the air-strikes of 21st November 1994, it was relatively quiet in my area." Could you tell me, first, what kind of air-strikes occurred in November 1994?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: In that period of time, NATO airplanes conducted air-strikes somewhere in the -- in the theatre, and the impact of that was that we really didn't know which way the situation from the military point of view concerning the UNMOs was going. It happened before and the UNMOs were in those periods that the air-strikes happened before really under pressure. And there was no telling at that time which way it was going to go with things like freedom of movement and the fact that we were deployed outside military barracks and living inside civilian areas. And during the first phase, we were ordered to stay in the house, and like I said, it was a difficult to say which way it was going to go. Eventually, the situation cleared up and we were allowed to do our job again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: These air-strikes --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: These air-strikes did not occur in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; in other words, not in the area of Sarajevo, if I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: No, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And that was the reason why your superiors gave you the order not to leave your compound. There were no other activities that would be dangerous to you, were there?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: No. The fact that we were ordered to stay in our accommodation did not come from the UNMO chain of command, who at that time was relative to the fact that the Bosniak army thought that for our safety it was better that we stayed in. We actually had a guard in front of our house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And that was always a member -- there was always a presence of the Bosnian army in Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And could you confirm just one more thing. This month of November was relatively quiet, wasn't it? At least that's in your statement.

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Well, as always -- the difference between things like the shelling which occurred in an instant and the things that we thought were regular military activities and those military activities were ongoing on a day to day basis especially on the Mount Igman road also referred as the logistic road going up or down Mount Igman in the BiH controlled pocket of Hrasnica. Other military activity was in that period relatively calm, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm primarily interested in shelling. Shelling targeted Hrasnica, right? Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, could you ask the witness -- could you ask the witness for how long they were ordered to stay inside their house in November 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Eimers. Could you explain to the Chamber for how long did you have to stay there under the guard placed outside your house by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: As I recall, it lasted three or four days, and then the tension seemed to have gone down and we were allowed to go out again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When I asked you a moment ago, and you did give me some sort of answer regarding this state of relatively quiet, I asked it in terms of shelling. Was it quiet in terms of shelling? There no shelling and therefore it was relatively quiet?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yes. From the point of shelling, it was relatively calm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Right. And just below this passage, the fourth paragraph on page 4 in English, page 5 in B/C/S, you said: "The BH army was preparing an attack on the southern part of Igman -- Mount Igman. The first actions that foreshadowed it started early recall in December south of the demilitarised zone." Now, could you describe to the Trial Chamber what were those first warring actions, as you put it in your statements -- statement, what were they like? What were they?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: The Bosnian army at the time prepared a ground strike in the direction of Gorazde, and they started the strike with long lasting mortar attacks in a non-occupied area, at least by civilians. There were a couple of military strong points on both sides of the Olympic road. The mortar attack lasted for a couple of hours, and then was followed by the ground move with - sorry for not counting - at least 200 soldiers. The attack lasted for, I believe, two or three days and then was cancelled by lack of success.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: They encountered resistance from the Bosnian Serb army. Is that logical?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Well, yes, it is. They attacked Bosnian Serb army-held terrain. They defended that, especially because it was in an area where there were no civilians living. It was just a military confrontation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, could we move to page 6 in B/C/S, which is English page 4, paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I just want to ask you one more thing in your first statement. Before that, could you tell me this: You mentioned Gorazde. Isn't this axis along which the BH army was attacking in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps facing Trnovo; and maybe if they had broken out, they would have reached Gorazde? Could you say that, because Trnovo was very close to you there?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, could you look at this paragraph where you say - that's on page 4, paragraph 6 in English - "As from 24th of December there was a cease-fire, so it was also a quiet period after that date." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, in the following passage, you speak about the first following major incident on the 18th of February, 1995.

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since you covered all the rest in your other statement of 13th October, 2006, I will move to that statement now, and that's Prosecution Exhibit P585.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be shown to the witness, please. It is his statement of the 13th of October, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that your statement, please?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at page 4 of the B/C/S version, and it is paragraph 8 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In that paragraph, you indicate where the house that you were staying in was situated in Hrasnica, and then you go on to say that: "From our post, we could see Ilidza and the road climbing up Mount Igman." Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours whether it is correct to say that Ilidza, which you mention here, is situated at the foot of Mount Igman and is under full control geographically of Mount Igman? Ilidza is in a valley?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time when you were posted in Sarajevo from October 1994 until April 1995, that was how it was throughout that period; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The separation line between the two parties was where the Famos factory was situated, and part of that factory was under the control of the BiH army and another part by the VRS. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yes. The confrontation line east of Hrasnica was actually in the -- inside the factory, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we say, then, as you are a military man, that for both sides that factory was a military target?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Since it was occupied by military only, I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From the position where your house was located as observers, did you have the full -- a full view of the area towards the tunnel going under the airport and a full view of the roads as well?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: From the house, we couldn't see the tunnel area because there was the township of Butmir in between; but from the rooftop of our house, actually from the bathroom, we could see up to the Mount Igman road to the west and we could see the Famos factory area to the east, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Hrasnica itself, and everything around you, you said a moment ago that some soldiers for a certain period were guarding your house and you couldn't come out. Was this mainly a location predominantly occupied by soldiers of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Well, no, it wasn't. They never came into the house. They always stayed outside in front of the house, and they would just make sure that basically we couldn't get out, expect for some administrative affairs, like getting food. We were allowed out to go to the market, but that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Eimers, that was a misunderstanding, I think. I wasn't referring to the people -- the soldiers standing in front of your house. I was meaning, generally speaking, in Hrasnica there was an entire brigade of the BiH army. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: That's correct. The 4th Brigade was in the Sokolovici/Hrasnica area. That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How many men roughly would there be there? I know that a brigade has a certain number. But according to your own knowledge what you were able to see roughly, how many troops were there?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Well, it was one of the reasons we were there, actually, but we were never able to establish an estimate on that. First of all, the soldiers were normal citizens during the day, and they moved during the night up to the military positions east and west and on Mount Igman. During the transition from their houses to the trenches, they weren't always wearing military clothes so it was very difficult to estimate whether they were actually during those moves doing soldier activities, military activities. The trenches, when they were occupied, not during the cease-fire period, that is, we were never allowed to see them. We were not allowed to get that near to the trenches or even talk to soldiers that were in the trenching during that time. So the estimate on how many soldiers there were actually in that valley, I cannot answer. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But can we say that because this was a military zone, a military area close to a very important place; that is, the separation line, that there weren't many -- or rather, the confrontation line, there weren't many civilians there, were there?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Well, the confrontation line in the west was in a very open terrain and there were hardly any civilians in that area; but on the east side, in the Famos factory area, the apartment buildings were maybe only 100 metres away from the Famos factory. So the civilians over there in the east were very close to the confrontation line. In the Mount Igman area, there were hardly any civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it implied that you mention that the 4th Brigade of the ABiH army was there that they this their facilities, command post, and everything that a military unit, called a brigade, needs to have, normally?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yes. The HQ of the 4th Brigade was actually in Sokolovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now move on to paragraph 14, please. It is page 7 of the B/C/S version and page 4 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So as not to spend too much time on it, can you just confirm that what it says here is true, that in most cases, especially in December, there was a cease-fire in force; and during that period of time, you mostly controlled the trenches, whether they were being expand, enlarged; that you entered the trenches of both sides; and there was nothing else apart from that. It was a relatively quiet period. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yes. We were especially tasked to outline the trenches from the beginning of the cease-fire so that we could control whether there was expansion or that there was just cleaning activities going on throughout the entire cease-fire period while it lasted until somewhere in the end of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I should now like to draw your attention to paragraph 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's page 8 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the end of that paragraph. If necessary, of course, can read through the whole paragraph, but I'm just asking you to focus on the end. In the English version, I think it goes on to the next page. So I should like to read to you the following: "The Bosnian army did nothing to protect civilians in the area of the tunnel and this protect the their operations." Does that mean that the BiH army, as is stated here, was using civilians to protect their military activities, as you have stated here?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you go on to say: "The nature of this tunnel was that it was used by both civilians and soldiers." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it right to say that every day there were people coming and going through that tunnel from Sarajevo. Quite a number of soldiers were passing through going in some various directions. Did you see that during your mission and stay there, in Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: I saw that on many occasions, yes, simply because we had to use the same road going into Sarajevo, as local military and civilians had to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 18, you point out that: "In Hrasnica, no one else was in control expect soldiers." Is that right, too?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you go on to say that: "In the winter of 1994 to 1995, they would withdraw from the United Nations." Who do you mean? The soldiers of the Bosnian army? Did you mean them?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: I have no idea what you mean actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Eimers, in paragraph 18, I have just read out what you stated about Hrasnica, and then you say: "In the winter of 1994/1995, they would withdraw from the United Nations because the Americans were supporting them with training and supplies." When you say "they," who do you mean? Do you mean soldiers of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: No. I mean the actually UN activities that were deployed over there; first of all, the UNMOs, but UNHCR and other agencies as well. So not the UN as an institution, but the UN agencies that were working in that area. The fact that they were supported by others meant that they were less depending on the guys that were already there; meaning, like I said, institutions like UNHCR or the UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Eimers, we are forced here to focus on military problems, and there is mention here of Americans supporting them with training. First of all, is it true that the Americans were assisting someone with training; if so, in what way?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: During the winter of 1994/1995, first of all --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I have an objection to the relevance of this line of questioning concerning the -- it has no bearing on the allegations in the amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure what it is leading to. Let me hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the winter of 1994/1995, it became obvious that the Bosniak army was getting support from other nations and by other means than we were used to, especially Americans were sighted. I contacted them myself on a number of occasions, and we witnessed American advisors with the Bosnian army high-rank officers in areas like the high ground of Mount Igman, obviously teaching them how to act military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you now look at the next paragraph, paragraph 19: "In October and November 1994, the Bosnians tried to break the siege from the Igman Olympic road area," as you said a moment ago; but then you add: "They fired 200 mortar shells as hour from Mount Igman." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then paragraph 21, you say there in the second sentence: "There was no proof of the existence of artillery guns inside Hrasnica, but they had mortars." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then further down, you say: "Both sides could handle the mortars very well." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: In my professional opinion, that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But in your first sentence, in paragraph 21, you say: "Once we were looking for a gun, but we never found it." The gun or cannon that you were looking for was it within the zone of responsibility of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: On a number of occasions, we got hearsay information that heavy weapons were used or at least moved in certain areas, and then we would be tasked to go after them. Like it's mentioned here, in Hrasnica, there was a one-time moment in which it was believed that there was an artillery piece in the area of Hrasnica itself. We were tasked to go after it, and we never found it. Mortars we did find occasionally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 22 in the B/C/S, that is page nine. You say in that paragraph: "The high ground, Mount Igman, was in Bosnian hands; whereas, the Serbs would fire at the end of the Mount Igman road from Ilidza." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then paragraph 24, you say that: "The Famos factory was the front line." You have already explained that, but I would like to inquire into the events that you describe as incidents that occurred while you were there. In paragraph 26, you refer to an incident that occurred on the 27th of February, 1995, when a woman, a civilian, was killed in Hrasnica; that is, in the area controlled by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But before I ask you about paragraph 26, can you confirm something that you explained in your first statement, that on the 18th of February in the morning, which means before the 27th of February, ten days before that on the 18th of February, three Serb soldiers were killed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Soldiers or civilians or the Serb side being killed, I never was able to confirm that in person. But we had UNMO teams deployed on the Serb side as well, and it was their task to confirm that. So the fact that Serbs had been killed in previous days was brought to me through chain of command, being the UNMO command, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And there's no question that this was during a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Like I stated somewhere else in -- in the text, it said that during the end of February, it was very clear to all parties that the cease-fire was not going to result in a final solution. The end of February was marked by several incidents, actually marking the beginning of the next phase of what might be described best as war; and in March, they really went off again. So the incidents described fit into that pattern, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you were describing this event of the 27th of February, you explained that. Is it true that the woman was killed in a house? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that that house was not directly hit; but several metres from that house, there was a tree and the shell hit the branches of that tree and then a fragment killed this woman in her apartment? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: That's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you confirm what you say in paragraph 26, and also in paragraph 7 of your first statement, that two Serb civilians were killed a day before that?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Well, I cannot confirm it. Only thing I can confirm is that that is what I was told, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I can finish the cross even before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So we come to paragraph 30. You say there, when talking about the period when you were in Vogosca: "Never, when I was present," and you're talking about the Serb side, "were there protests about civilians being killed." First, can you tell us, were there civilians casualties in Vogosca while you were there?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Well, yes, there was. The only event that I can elaborate on is like it is described in article 30, saying that an 80-year-old man was killed in the suburbs of Vogosca when he was walking in the fields, and that is the only thing, the only event that could be proved while I was there, especially because later on we happened to run into funeral. But like it is stated, most of the time, as far as I know all of the time, we were not reported civilians being killed on the BSA side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You testified to this yourself. You said, in the statement, they did not protest, the Serbs did not protest about this. They would bury their people without making any protests. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 31. Here you explain events along the logistics route, which went from the tunnel next to Hrasnica, through Hrasnica towards Igman. You say in paragraph 31: "The army of the Bosnian Serbs firing from Ilidza with anti-aircraft rockets would hit civilian vehicles on the road." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you go on to say: "The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina did use civilian vehicles along this road for logistic purposes for both military and civilian purposes." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: That's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "One could not tell whether there were civilians or military in those vehicles." Can you confirm that, too?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yeah. That's correct, simply because the vehicles moved at night; and during the day-time, there was hardly any traffic. So the -- it was always dark when the vehicles came down or went up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In any event, in most cases, these were vehicles that were being used for military purposes.

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say -- or at least I can't prove that it was in most cases. But the vehicles that went up served two purposes; military and civilian. The -- a lot of vehicles that used this road were to supply Sarajevo in the broader sense, especially the civilian necessities. Yes, it was used for military purposes as well, and sometimes they used the same vehicle for both purposes at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: A little further down, you explain something when you say: "In my time in Sarajevo, I never saw tanks in Sarajevo." But then you say, and I quote: "There were trucks with machine-guns on the back, light and heavy anti-aircraft guns." Is that true, too?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there trucks going into the direction of Igman and coming from Sarajevo, and because there were machine-guns on them and light and heavy anti-aircraft guns were the target of fire?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. The only time we actually witnessed the heavy machinery being there was on the BSA side in the Ilidza area. We never witnessed heavy military equipment being brought up or down through the logistic road on Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But if you would look at another sentence in that same paragraph, and I quote, could you explain that for us, please. "This was not a factor that would be taken into consideration during attacks on the logistic road. These weapons were concerned to be heavy weapons." You're talking here about the logistic road going to Igman and about heavy weaponry going along that route. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: No, that's not right. I mention only the heavy equipment being used by the BSA from Ilidza to fire at the logistic road, and we never have gotten any proof that the heavy weapons that may have been in use by the Bosnian army were taken through that route as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 38, please. You refer to paragraph 17 in your first statement. That is the incident of the 18th of February, 1995, and that was the date when the three Serb soldiers were killed. Let us see how you refer to it here. You say that: "The weather was getting better and military activity started to proceed again, though it was officially still a cease-fire period." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then you added: "The Serbs started blaming the United Nations for everything the Bosnian were doing." Is that so?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yes. It was the time where both parties started their strategic moves towards who was to blame for an official ending of the cease-fire, and this went on and on on a day-to-day basis at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And could we also clear up what you say in paragraph 44, and that would complete my cross-examination. Mr. Eimers, you left on the 4th of April, left Hrasnica that is. Around that date, around the 4th of April, were there quite -- was there quite a lot of conflict between the two warring sides? Did the BH army achieve certain results in relation to the positions it held around the Famos factory during your stay there?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: No. I think that especially the -- the way the trenches were laid out and the situation in the Famos factory was that the -- the war in the sense of gaining ground had come to a complete standstill, and that the fighting in those areas was just to make sure that everybody knew that they were still there, both sides did. Sometimes there is was fierce fighting, but in the end I think everybody knew that it was not going to get to any military result in those areas. Everybody knew that the areas that the areas that may have been more suited for a military attack that should lead to big success were in other areas around Sarajevo and not in the Hrasnica area itself. So, at that time, there was a really breakout of war again, but I don't think that the Hrasnica area was an area where both parties expected success at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand what you are saying. But as you were in Hrasnica, you said here in your first sentence: "In paragraph 20 of my first statement, I describe an all-out attack with all kinds of weaponry being fired that started a few days before I left." Is that correct? Does that mean that before you left, those few days before you left, what I have just read out was happening?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you say towards the end, and that brings me to my last question. Allow me to read it all. I quote: "During the winter, the Bosnian army was supported and equipped by the Americans. We saw them doing reconnaissance all over Sarajevo to see whether they would succeed. This became a massive attack to Vogosca to the north, to break the siege, which failed." Is all this correct, what you have said here, both with respect to the assistance of the Americans, and the attack through Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Like I stated before, I'm 100 per cent sure that there was a huge American involvement during the winter; and, yes, the attack from the north to break the siege started just after I left; and, yes, it failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Eimers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, are you going to re-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I have two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Major Eimers, I want to clear up one point. The first time I was asking you questions, we went through your experience with mortars as a Dutch officer. You remember that. And then at the beginning of the cross-examination, Mr. Tapuskovic asked you, "Well, isn't it so that you have more experience with mortars today than he did back then." Do you remember this exchange?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: In the 12 years since you have left Sarajevo, and the 12 additional years of professional experience that you have gained, has anything about that experience caused you to change the opinions you have expressed today or the opinions that are in the statements that have been introduced into evidence?

utterances.speaker: RONALD EIMERS
utterances.text: No, I haven't. It has just been made more clear to me that what I witnessed during my stay in Sarajevo was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Major Eimers, that concludes your testimony. We thank you for giving it, and you may now leave. We'll take the break now. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. Mr. Whiting, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Could you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Berko Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your first name is Berko?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Berko Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, do you have a copy of a report that you wrote in connection with this case at the request of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you can open it up. It's that report in front of you.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, the 65 ter number of this report is 3118, and I would ask that it be given an exhibit number at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes P586.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to use the e-court system to go to pages of this report because it's my understanding that everybody in the courtroom; Your Honours, the legal officers, the Defence, the accused, the witness, ourselves, the interpreters, the court reporter, everybody has a copy of the report in their own language. If I could just confirm that, before I proceed. I see no dissenting nods or shakes of the head, so I will proceed that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Professor Zecevic, I'm focussing on the first chapter of your report where you set out your qualifications. I'm going to quickly go through your qualifications; and unless there is an objection, I'm just going to summarize them and ask if you agree that I have summarized them correctly. From the 1st of August, 1975, until May of 1992, you worked at the Pretis factory in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Da. [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That factory produced artillery and rocket ammunition and aircraft bombs. You worked in the research and development centre, and your primary fields of work were rocket motors and warheads and developing new rocket projectiles; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Also, since 1976, you have been a member of the faculty at Sarajevo University's Faculty of Mechanical Engineering; first in the Mechanics Department and at a later date in the Department of Defence Technology. You are still a member of that faculty today. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In 1992, May of 1992, you left Pretis and became the Deputy Commander of the Centre for Military Industry within the Main Staff of the ABiH and that ceased to exist in mid-1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: At the end of 1993 until mid-August of 1994, you were employed by Unis, which did research of weapons and armaments for the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During the war, you were tasked specifically with investigating two incidents in Sarajevo; the shelling of the Markale market on the 5th of February, 1994, which is now known as Markale 1, and the air bomb incident at the TV tower on the 28th of June, 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Professor, aside from those two incidents where you were specifically tasked with investigating, did you have other occasions during the war to observe the effects of air bombs or other weapons?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you give us an estimate of -- of how frequently or how many times you observed that?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: For personal reasons, because my profession has to do with ammunitions and their testing, logically I was interested in practical use of weapons, not in testing conditions only. Since I lived in Sarajevo at the time when it was constantly exposed to shelling by mortar and rocket systems, the things that I had learned before the war from books could be seen in practice. I first had occasion to see in January 1994, at the invitation of one of my students, an occasion to see the remnants of one rocket propelled bomb. In 1995, when there were more frequent incidents in the vicinity of my house at the distance of 500 to 1.000 metres, there were several impacts of such projectiles. I went out on site to see the effects. I will not speak of artillery and mortar projectiles that were a daily occurrence on the entire area of Sarajevo, and every time I walked around town I had occasion to see detonations of such projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Professor, for your benefit, or for the benefit of everyone else in the courtroom, I'm going to tell you how I'm going to conduct my examination today. I am going to divide it into three parts. The first part will be to talk briefly about how modified air bombs were constructed and what types existed during the war. The second part will be to talk more specifically about some of the characteristics of modified air bomb; for example, their range, their accuracy, matters such as that. And then the third and final part will be to go through all of the specific incidents that you analyse in your report that are related to our indictment. There are, I believe, 11 in all. We will briefly go through each one to talk about the conclusions that you reached. Now, turning to the first matter, I want to talk about how air bombs were constructed, modified air bombs. First, could you tell us what kinds of bombs were used to conduct modified air bombs, and here I am focussing on what types of explosive charges in these bombs were used.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, in the period of 1994/1995, three types of modified air bombs were registered. Two of them were manufactured in Pretis factory before the war, and another type, from my knowledge and from insight into the remnants, was manufactured in Russia. The first was a modified air bomb OBAD-500. It had four rocket mortars enabling it to be launched at a range of 3.5 to 4 kilometres. It had fuel air explosive and a very complex system for identifying the moment of impact; several types of fuses; and it was effective in the area where it fell. The other two types were FAB-100, where the standard body of a 100-kilogram bomb was used. FAB was a Russia acronym for "Fugasnaya Aviatsionnaya Bomba," and another type had a mass -- and the number 400 in the name meant it weighed 100 kilograms. It had a rocket motor, and its range was five to six kilometres. Most of the bombs that fell in the environment of Sarajevo or inside Sarajevo of this type had TNT that is solid explosive charge. The other bomb, FAB-250, which weighed roughly 250 kilograms, was for the most part equipped with three rocket motors, had a range of close to eight kilometres; and from what I know and from what I had occasion to see with my own eyes in Sarajevo, it did not use solid explosive charge. It used fuel air explosive instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in that answer, you talked about two different types of explosive charges, of the -- solid explosive charge or TNT and the fuel air explosive charge. Could you describe briefly for the Trial Chamber what the differences are between these two explosive mechanisms or charges on impact. What differences do they produce when they explode?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Differences are huge. When it detonates, an air bomb with the solid explosive such as TNT pressures are created inside the bomb of 200 to 250.000 bars. That is a temperature of four to 5.000 degrees centigrade. A blast wave is created in detonation of very high intensity, but its characteristic is with the increase of distance from the centre of explosion its effects diminish. In addition to the so-called blast effect, a bomb equipped with sold explosive charge, TNT, has a prominent fragmentation effect, because a bomb like FAB-250 should have 20.000 fragments of various sizes. They move at a velocity of 1.800 to 2.000 metres per second and can create vast devastation against humans and structures even very far from the centre of explosion. Speaking of bombs with fuel air explosives, the concept is very different. A bomb -- the bomb is equipped with a substance that is primarily fuel. It does not contain an oxidator, and that bomb is destroyed before it takes effect. The liquid inside the bomb disperses in the air, mixes with the air, and only then are secondary fuses activated, which activate the detonation process in several points in the surrounding area. What is also important is the pressure during the detonation of such a bomb, pressure of ten, 20, 30 bars. But the area of that overpressure effect is very large, and it has very large lethal effects on human bodies and surrounding structures. And as you could notice from the war in Iraq in 1991 and 2002, such bombs played a very important role in the destruction of structures and tunnels.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Professor, you -- in that last answer, you said that the a TNT or solid explosive charge produces an enormous number of fragments on explosion, some 20.000. Does a fuel-air bomb produce any fragments?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A fuel-air bomb also produces familiarities, because in order for the liquid to go out of the body, the body has to be destroyed, which means that a smaller quantity of solid explosive also has to be used. That also coughs fragmentation, although fragments have smaller velocity, a smaller range, and they don't really have any function in the lethal effect against structures and humans. Their primary role is as a consequence of the destruction of the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in an earlier answer, when you described that there were three types of bombs modified into modified air bombs, you said that two of them were produced at Pretis. Could you tell us which two were produced at Pretis, just so we're clear?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's FAB-100 and FAB-250.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when these bombs were produced at Pretis -- first of all, when did they first start being produced at Pretis, what year, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I came there to Pretis in 1975, and already it was serially manufactured. If we look at the code of FAB-100 bomb, we see M173. In Yugoslavia, it was customary that when a certain new weapon is introduced in the arsenal, it gets a code that indicates the year it was introduced. So we have 75, 80, et cetera. There are several variants with modified shapes, but this bomb was certainly produced in 1975.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when it was produced then in 1975 and the years later, what was its intended mode of delivery; that is, how was it going to be dropped or launched on a target at that time? How was that designed and intended?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The very name, aircraft bomb, tells us about the intent. The idea was that a fighter plane carries a number of bombs that are dropped from either a high altitude or from high velocity flight. So the bomb would be dropped from an aircraft, fuses were activated, and the bomb would drop in free-fall or it have a breaking chute system to reduce possible negative effects for the carrying aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I interrupted you. Okay. That's fine. That's sufficient. Thank you. When did these bombs, the FAB-100 and the FAB-250, start to be modified so that they could be launched from the ground rather than being dropped from an aeroplane.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My first encounter with it was in 1993 in the theatre of operations close to Vogosca. That's when the first -- when one FAB-100 was first launched. In 1995, I had occasion to see an FAB-250. From the documents that I had opportunity to find in the Pretis factory, after the war, I saw that sometime in February 1994, there was a first reference to the development of two launchers for modified bombs by the military technical -- Military Engineering Institute from Belgrade. But I want to emphasise that my first real encounter with fuel-air rocket propelled bombs was in January 1994. In 1994, more intense work was carried out in the vicinity of Sarajevo on the modification of aircraft bombs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you in a position to say whether these bombs had been modified anywhere else in the world before that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a Russia bomb, OBAD-500, used in Chechnya that was modified. Later in 2004 and 2005, the Russians modified this system and produced a new system, Boran or TS-1. The initial intention of the Russians was to use fuel-air bombs in order to neutralise minefields in areas where their troops would be moving. And my opinion is that one of the types of those bombs that were modified at the time and that were used in Chechnya in the 1990s was for the first time used to target Sarajevo in January 1994. You can find in reports on Chechnya, references to intensive use of fuel-air rocket propelled bombs against the town of Grozni. In my opinion, the modification of aircraft bombs, FAB-250, was an attempt to create the KREMA-4 Russian bomb. It was based on OBAD-500 bomb equipped with four rocket motors of the GRAD system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So the conflict in Sarajevo would not have been the first time that these bombs were modified so that they could be launched from the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only speak to Sarajevo, Mr. President, and the information I had then, in 1994 and 1995. I was under siege in that town, and I had no other information. I can only speak about Sarajevo, and I can speak about the things that can be found in reports of the Red Cross, Helsinki Watch, and other NGOs that were wrote about the events in Chechnya. There are no photographs of remnants found in Chechnya. There were only photographs of Soviet rocket-propelled bombs found in Sarajevo, and such examples can be found elsewhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina and a part in the Netherlands, because the Dutch army transferred some of the non-operative rocket-propelled systems to the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just follow-up on the President's question. Professor, do you know how the people at the Pretis factory developed the technique of modifying air bombs so as to be able to launch them from the ground. I guess what was under lying the President's question was really, did the people at Pretis were they inspired by the Russians? Did they get the idea from Russia, or were they somehow assisted by the Russians in developing this new technique?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to draw your attention to the fact that the Pretis factory just before the war in 1990, 1991, and 1992 was developing the fuel-air bomb. So the process of development had already started at the time. It's just that fuel-air bomb was not supposed to be launched by rockets. It was supposed to be dropped from an aircraft. In the 1970s, work was done on developing a fuel-air mine or shell that was to have been deployed on possible axis of attack by the Soviet Union, because Yugoslavia was under the pressure of this possibility of being attacked by rocket air-strikes from the Soviet Union. I know a professor from the Rocket Institute who studied in America, and he had occasion to get acquainted with rocket explosives used by Americans in Vietnam. He with his research department, and in cooperation with the Pretis factory, participated in the development of this fuel-air bomb. The whole project was transferred to Belgrade later, and Pretis stopped working on it. As more modification, it is my deep conviction that people, engineers from Pretis, accepted the idea and the concept that they had seen on Russian systems, and they tried to apply that concept in their project. The Russian system was very complex and very sophisticated in terms of design, and it was very time-consuming and very costly. In Pretis, people did not have such resources, but they have very capable.
