And within their possibilities at the time, within the energy and resources they had, they tried to achieve a certain improvement over what existed before. And there is, of course, a huge difference in quality between the two bombs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Professor, thank you for your clarification. I understand you to say that the people at Pretis were inspired by what they saw in Russia; namely, of developing a technique to launch an air bomb from the ground; but because of the way the Russians had developed their project, the Pretis people could not do that because they did not have the same resources. So they developed -- they just worked further on the idea and developed it further and found a simpler solution by attaching rockets to it. Is that a correct understanding? Because the Chamber needs to know how was the thing developed in Pretis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I attach some importance, Mr. Whiting, to the issue of the history of the development of the modified air bomb, because in my view it can have an impact on the question of intent. If the technique was initiated by the Bosnian Serbs or whether they borrowed the technique from elsewhere, and that's why I asked the question which I did, which was been followed up by Judge Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I can certainly pursue that with further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness can help us to the extent that he can, but if he can't take us any further than he has already testified, then so be it for the time being. But do you have anything more to say on that matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me try to answer the Honourable Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Russian system, KREMA, also has rocket motors. The modified projectile, FAB-250, has rocket motors, so they have very similar in concept. But the rocket system on FAB-250, on the aircraft bomb FAB-250, is simpler. It doesn't have close range fuel. It doesn't have secondary fuses. It has no parachute brakes because there were no resources and no time to perfectly copy or to copy to perfection the Russian concept. That's at least how I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just to follow-up to some extent on these questions. When you left the Pretis factory in 1992, was there any work or any thought being given to modifying aircraft bombs in this way; that is, attaching rockets so that they could be launched from the ground?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. There was no idea of that kind at the time. We, at that time, were only working on a particular bomb for neutralising air fields, air strips. We were copying the French bomb, Durendal, a penetration bomb. There were no mention of avio bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you gave your answer with respect to Pretis. In your position at Pretis, did you become aware of any work being down to modify aircraft bombs anywhere else in the former Yugoslavia, so that they could be launched with rockets from the ground.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Up to 1992, there was a clear division of labour as to who did what. Pretis was in charge of developing air systems and guidance systems and air bombs. Licki Osik, which was within Unis, did its own work. So the answer to your question is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just to be clear, I'm going to try to state one more time what I think your answer is. It's your view that when in late 1993 or early 1994, development began on modifying these aircraft bombs so they could be launched from the ground, and that the people who did that at Pretis were following the Russian example, were trying to copy what the Russians had done. Is that a fair characterisation of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I am sorry. I didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Quite. Quite. It's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that in this case my learned friend Mr. Whiting directly led the witness in terms of what the expert was supposed to say as his own expert opinion, whereas Mr. Whiting directly put the response to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I can't agree with you, because we have been discussing this matter with the witness for the past ten minutes and he has already said that. So Mr. Whiting merely asked him to confirm whether that was his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Professor, you -- excuse me. You stated earlier that the FAB-100 air bomb was modified with a single rocket and the FAB-250 was modified with three rockets. Now, just drawing your attention to page 68 of your report in the B/C/S. It's page 73 in the English. Could you just tell us what types of rockets were used to modify the FAB-250?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It can be noticed that there were few types of rocket motors that were used for propelling the FAB-250. The GRAD 122-millimetre was used the most and then the M70 Oganj and 127-millimetre K13, which is from a guided rocket, or rather, missile. So there were three types of rocket motors that were primarily used to propel the FAB-250 bomb. Every one of these rocket boosters had different performance, so this significantly affected the performance of the bombs so there were no uniform characteristics. That is what I wish to say. I'm speaking in terms of range and dispersion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, when you say that the 127-millimetre K13 is a guided rocket or missile, what do you mean by that? In what way was it guided?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, these were Russian missiles that were a copy of US missiles; and since they had become obsolete, they were supposed to be destroyed before the war. However, as the situation developed in Yugoslavia as the war started, these rocket motors were used to propel this air bomb. So just the rocket motor -- the rocket booster was without a guidance system.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you touched on this a little bit in some of your earlier answers, but could you tell us, based on your analysis and your expertise, can you comment on the professional standards that were achieved in the modifications of these aircraft bombs so that they could be launched from the ground? And this is -- just for everyone's, benefit, this is touched on page 74 of the report in English, page 68 in B/C/S. What professional standards -- what kind of professionalism was achieved in modifying these air bombs; the FAB-100 and the FAB-250.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I have to say that a professional -- or rather, the professional level attained in this production did not equal that of the Russian system. There are many inconsistencies involved. Therefore, its performance is of lesser quality and, therefore, it cannot be propelled to the targets where it is supposed to be propelled. So its accuracy is at a lower level. If we look at this study, you can see that there are enormous differences in systems of centering of rocket motors. There are enormous differences in terms of placing stabilisers on projectiles --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm just going to interrupt you for a second, because I see that you are on page 69 of your version of the report where there are some pictures. On page 69 -- I think it's the next page, and that's page 75 in the English and the figure 98?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The picture on the left is the FAB-250, and on the right is the Russian system the OBAD-500. Can you just very briefly give specific differences in terms of quality between these two systems. In what way -- what specific ways do you say that the FAB-250 was of a lesser quality.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two basic objections to be raised here. One is in terms of centering the rocket motors, because the rocket motor creates a force that propels the projectile. At the moment, when rocket motors are not properly centred, then the projectile deviates. In the Russian system, there is a direct link among adjacent rocket motors, which makes it is able to compensate for pressure. In this way, there is a uniform force involved; whereas, in the modified Pretis system, there is it no interconnection between the rocket motors. So every rocket motor had a different type of pressure, which could affect its stability. Furthermore, the centering of rocket motors of the Russian system was carried out through certain surfaces that were the basis for the whole system; whereas, as far this other system in Pretis was concerned, it was done through a simple triangular system among the rocket motors, and then further on the stabiliser that are the basic - how should I put this? - the basic point that makes it is possible for the projectile to reach the place it is supposed to reach. It was not done with great accuracy at Pretis, and it could even be moved while it was being launched. So there were many incomplete things in the design of the system, things that should have been worked on in order to improve the system. I'm surprised at that, because in Pretis there were a great many qualified engineers, qualified workers, and there was proper equipment. The only justification for this can be time to have a system developed as fast as possible, not looking at the possible effects in terms of this system being unreliable, in terms of its launching, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Or might it have been done deliberately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so. I cannot imagine that. I cannot imagine professionals doing that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Professor, just to follow-up on what you just said about time. Based on your long experience and expertise, can you tell the Trial Chamber how long does it typically take to develop a new weapon system?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This kind of system? Not less than five to seven years of intensive work, with all available resources, with a great many tests that were to be carried out on hundreds of such projectiles or even a thousand such projectiles, so that it could be certified for use in a modern army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Professor, even to achieve the substandard level of quality that you have described, with respect to the FAB-250 and the FAB-100, can you tell us was it technically easy to construction these weapons or technically difficult? Give us some sense of the difficulty from a technical point of view of making this modification to an aircraft bomb.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If you look at the dimensions, it's three metres. That's the length of the rocket. 360 kilograms is its mass. It is an enormous object, if I can call it that. Is it extremely complex to manipulate something like that. Modification is not an easy job in this sense. It calls for manpower, energy, know-how. Pretis could produce the body but not the fuel. So fuel had to be imported. Fuel could not be obtained in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It had to be imported to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Fuses are complex. So it should also be noted that the Bugojno factory was under control of the HOV. So in order to use multiple fuses, they had to be imported from elsewhere or constructed there, but it could not be done in Pretis; and then also the metal tin that could not be produce in the Bosnia-Herzegovina. It had to be imported into Bosnia-Herzegovina. This required a broad-based effort of the entire military industry, which was under the control of the army of Republika Srpska at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, moving to another topic, and we're moving to chapter 14 of your report, which is page 97 in the English and 88 in the B/C/S. Can you describe for us briefly how these modified air bombs were launched?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: From available video material that I had occasion to see, and from what was seen at the exhibition in 2001 in Belgrade, one can see that this was a launcher that was made on the TAM-100 truck that had a system which made it possible to direct the barrels horizontally and vertically. So an appropriate launching angle could be obtained, and also it was possible to adjust the azimuth. Every one of these systems can be seen on the photographs. You can see the FAB-100 rocket-assisted bombs had four guide-rail for launching them, and also you can see the FAB-250 rocket-assisted bombs. They were launched with two guide-rail. So it's a relatively simple launcher, not very accurate, because it doesn't have a stabilising system in terms of the horizontal position. However, if we look at its performances, it is quite satisfactory for this kind of guiding. I must say that six metres is the length of the barrel of the launcher because that was required in order to attain appropriate stability for the projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What methods would you have with this launcher to aim the direction of the modified aircraft bomb? You referred to horizontal/vertical and to the azimuth. Can you just explain that very briefly again?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The azimuth makes it is possible for us to direct ourselves to the objective. If I'm supposed to target that door, I'm going to have my launching system face that door, taking into account rotation, whether it is going to be left or right. If I want to be accurate in hitting the area around the door, I have to lift the elevation; that is to say, to lift the guide-rail under a certain angle, and the tables have to define that. So once I have got that right, the azimuth and the elevation; and then if I also take into account atmospheric data, because these rockets are say are very sensitive to temperature, air humidity, then I think that I can get the target I want. That would be it in the briefest possible terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We'll talk more about that later getting the target that you want. I want to stay for one moment on the launching system. You made a reference to video. The photographs that you have in chapter 14 of your report, do they have any relationship to a video.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And have you seen that video?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to play the video for you at this time. I think if we watch it on e-court and if we switch to Sanction, hopefully this will work. It's about one minute long. It has a brief speaking, but the English translation will appear on the bottom of the screen. We're not getting sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Professor, while we're getting the sound, can you just tell us what it is that is depicted in this video.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This video footage depicts the placing of an air bomb, FAB-100, on the launching system. First, an elevation was taken, then the air bomb; that is to say, without the rocket motors, was placed on the guide-rail; and then at the bottom of the air bomb, the rocket motor was attached; then the azimuth was taken, which is necessary procedure, and then the air bomb was launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We'll try it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Already at this moment I would have to object. This can only be used as an illustration. The Prosecutor had to tell us at least where this had been used. This was used somewhere in Krajina. Does it have anything to do with the Sarajevo front?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, yes, tell us about the provenance of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, the provenance is actually from the witness. The witness relied upon this in his report as a source for showing how these air bombs were launched. I'm not suggesting for a moment that this depicts an air bomb being launched in Sarajevo or anywhere near Sarajevo. That is not the purpose at all. It is simply for the technical purposes of seeing how these operate, and that is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where is it in the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's in chapter 14. You will see that the photographs in the chapter 14 are stills from this video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do we have sound? We're getting assistance for the sound, I think. I think what we will they're working on this I will move on to my next set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We'll get back to this and hopefully have an opportunity to see the launching of an air bomb. And I will move to the second area of question, and that is to talk about some of the specific characteristics of the air bomb which is relevant to our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: First of all, the range -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Of course, once I get halfway through my next question -- it's working. Let's give it a try. That was premature. I'll go back to my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Professor, what the range was of the FAB-100 and the FAB-250, and this is at page 83 of your report in English and page 75 to 76 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The range of the FAB-100 was about 5.560 metres; whereas, the range of the FAB-250 was about 7.680 metres. I'm talking about maximum range. There is a logical caution that has to be made. Often, other rocket motors were used. These performances could slightly vary. So in this case, I oriented myself towards the GRAD 122-millimetres, and I took their values in nominal terms; the ones I had, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, since you are familiar with miles, what is 5.560 metres in miles?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm familiar with miles but not so much with metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. We'll have somebody work that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll do the math.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Five miles, roughly a, bit less. That is the FAB-250. And three point something, about three and a half miles is the FAB-100.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Your expertise has, once again, come into assistance. Okay. Now, the case manager promises me that it is working. So I will interrupt this line of questioning, which we will come back to, so that we could watch this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm just going to interrupt for a moment there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Here the men in the video appear to be screwing something in. Can you tell us what they're doing here?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. The men appear in the video to be screwing something in. Can you tell us what they're doing? Are you getting a translation?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's fine now. These four men are trying to place the rocket motor into the back part of the FAB-100, in order to create a link between the rocket motor and the body of the bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We'll continue now with the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, could that video clip be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let's hear first from Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think my learned friend Mr. Whiting should explain why this is important. Why is this relevant? When did we ever discuss that five seconds is necessary to fire a certain number of rockets. Eighteen rockets in five seconds, what is the relevance to our case? Is this technique an appropriate subject with this expert that is supposed to deal with specific situations? It was never discussed that this power was used on the Sarajevo front line where 18 rockets should be fired in five seconds. I think the expert should concentrate on his own subject; the modified air bomb that was fired one at a time perhaps. This may be with an educational experience, but it certainly does not help us with the specific cases in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reference to 18 rockets being fired fire seconds has really no bearing. That is not the purpose for which I offer the video clip. I don't think there is any dispute that the incidents in the indictment were essentially single-shot incidents. The video clip is relevant because, number one, it shows the mechanism and how these rockets were operated, how they were launched, how they were put together, how they were constructed, how they looked, which is the subject or one of the subjects of this report. This was relied upon and it is contained in the report. And then, secondly, it is obviously directly relevant because you see a launching of one of these rockets, which is also an issue in our indictment. So I think it is certainly sufficiently relevant so that it can be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we agree. We admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P587, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Professor that was a launching of a -- well, let me ask you this: The launching that we see there is that a single rocket or is that multiple rockets being launched.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This was a launching of only one rocket, although we see on the launcher that there are four rockets placed. What we saw was the launching of only one rocket; whereas, there are four placed on the launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you compare for us in terms of the -- the sound and the smoke and the fire of the launching. Would a launching of a FAB-250 have more or less sound, smoke, and fire at the time of launching?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have to specify this. When you fire a large range rocket, 150 kilometres, the effects are much more powerful when you fire several than when you fire one. However, the launching of FAB-250 creates noise. It's possible that it creates even smoke, but that depends on the temperature of the air, the humidity, the presence of trees around, the presence of structures. If there are any structures around, the intensity of noise created by launching is muffled. We hear a high-pitched noise as the rocket moves while the rocket booster is active, and the part along which the rocket booster is active is around 450 metres. If the maximum range is 6.2 kilometres, the rocket booster only works for 400 metres, which means that in some cases launching is audible; whereas, in other cases there is almost no noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Professor, my question is actually more simple than that. If you compare the launching of a single FAB-100 and the launching of a single FAB-250, under the same conditions from the same spot, how would they compare in terms -- just at the moment of launch, in terms of sound, smoke, fire. Would one have more of that than the other, or would they be the same?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's possible the noise could be more intensive because three rocket boosters were used in FAB-250 and only one in FAB-100. The time of activity of the rocket booster also differs between the two bombs. The noise would be more intensive and the flames.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go back to talk about the range of the FAB-100 and the FAB-250, and I'm going to draw your attention to page 84 of the English and page 76 of the B/C/S. And here you say that the maximum range, as you have already testified, of the FAB-250 is 7.680 metres; and then you go on to say that it's effective range is 5.820 metres to 7.680 metres. Can you explain for us, please, what do you mean by "effective range"?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand effective range to mean one characteristic of rocket propelled projectiles. With smaller angles, there would be ricochet, which means that when the projectile impacts on the ground, if angle of descent is small, the projectile does not get buried in the ground. It ricochets and the fuse is not activated, for the reason that the fuse placed on those aircraft bombs was small in length. So before impacting on a flat surface, and I emphasise flat surface, the body hits the ground before the fuse gets in contact with the ground, which is the reason for the ricochet. Through geometrical analysis, I determined that ricochet become possible at angle of 25 degrees, and that' why I said the limit was 5.820. But if the bomb hits in a pit or a vertical wall, it will be effective, even with a smaller angle of descent. So the range could be 4.000 metres, 4.500 metres. So when we say "effective range," we mean on a flat surface, not in an urban area, not a bumpy surface. So in town, since you have a lot of structures, range could have been smaller.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When we use "effective range," in our terminology, we mean on a flat surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Are you able to give an effective -- an estimation of the effective range for the FAB-250 if you're using it in an urban setting where, as you say, you have either a bumpy surface or buildings. You said it would be less than 5.820 on the lower end. Are you able to give an estimate of the effective range?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Incontestably. I just want to draw your attention to this. When a projectile moves through the air --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- the range could be on the order of 4.000 metres. It can be 3.000 metres. There is no reason why not, if it's going to hit a vertical target.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Did the launching system of the modified aircraft bombs put any limitations on the angle that they could be launched from? And here I'm looking at page 99 of your report in English and 90 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, certainly, it is on the characteristics of the launcher that both the minimal and maximum angle depend. We see on these photos that the angle is -- depends on the size of the truck and the height of the carrying platform. So every launcher has its own performances in terms of adjusting elevation and adjusting the azimuth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, at page 99 in the English and page 90 of the B/C/S, you -- you say that the range of possible adjustment for elevation was between 20 degrees and 50 degrees.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How does that effect the effective range of the FAB-250; that is, what would be the range, approximate range at 20 degrees, and what would the approximate range fired at 50 degrees, If you are able to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If the launcher would take an elevation of 50 degrees, the range would be less than the said 7680. It would be shorter, say, 7.000. But if the elevation is 20 degrees, then the range would be slightly less than 5.000 metres, with an elevation of 20 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just so we're clear on this: At what elevation do you achieve the maximum change?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We usually take 45 degrees to be the one enabling the greatest range.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Let's talk now about accuracy. In your report - it's in chapter 4 - you describe different ways of measuring the accuracy of a weapon. And I don't want to go into too much detail about this because it is set out at length in your report, but could you just briefly tell the Trial Chamber what is meant by "circular error probability," sometimes referred to as CEP? What does that mean, in just two sentences?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In military use of weapon systems, you usually have to focus to where the launch projectiles would fall, and that's how you calculate how many projectiles need to be fired to fit the target. And in keeping with that, we use the term "circular error probability," which determines that if 50 per cent of projectiles fired fall into that area with a certain radius, let's say, R, then we say that the projectile has a dispersion defined by the circular error probability. It doesn't mean that all projectiles launched will necessarily fall in that area. It means that only 50 per cent will; whereas, the other 50 percent will disperse across a much boarder area. So if we say that the radius is 100 metres, then 50 per cent of the projectiles will fall within their radius of 100 metres and the others will fall outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's an estimate of the dispersion of the projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to talking specifically about the FAB-100 and FAB-250, and if you would turn, please, to page 73 of the report in B/C/S, page 79 to 80 in the English. Now, you say -- you say that with a FAB-100, it is only possible to target a surface area measuring 500 metres by 200 metre. That's at page 79 of the English, page 73 of the B/C/S. And then turning to the next page in English, and staying on the same page in B/C/S, you say with the FAB-250, it is only possible to target a surface area measuring 600 metres by 250 metres. Now explain for us, bearing in mind the terminology that you have just explained, what is meant by that. What do you mean it is possible to target a surface area of those dimensions?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When unguided missiles are used, such as artillery, mortar, rockets, you can never fire at a single target. That's what guided missiles are for. If you wanted to, as I said before, hit a certain target in Sarajevo, it is extremely improbable, except by accident, that a single individual missile will hit that target. That's why I put in my report "by using a volley of fire. " It was necessary, in other words, to fire a number of rockets that would fall around the target and possibly, with the assistance of the warhead, destroy the target. The chance to hit the target directly is minimal. It's common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's focus a little more on the specific area that you give. For example, with the FAB-250, you say it's possible to target a surface area measuring 600 metres by 250 metres. Are you able to tell us if the FAB-250 is fired from its effective range, how many of the projectile would say you expect to fall within that area of 600 metres by 250 metres, and how many would you expect to fall outside of that area? Are you able to give us that information?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It would be frivolous on my part to venture such an estimate, because there are no reference performances that would enable conclusions. I made certain assumptions that are usual in making estimates, and I said that with a certain mass the effective range is 350 metres. If you change the mass, by 12.5 kilograms, then possible deflection from the target is 350 metres if you change the propelling force of the rocket booster. And every rocket booster is different. It has to be strictly controlled, and you have no which particular rocket boosters are built in the system. And that is something that we didn't know, because we bought them from abroad. They were old, ten to 15-years-old. And if there is just a small change of impulse and a small change in air temperature, just ten degrees, then the point of impact is changed by 90 metres. Those are just certainly parameters used to illustrate how sensitive the firing system of this projectile is. And based on these parameters, I said that with a range of 600 metres, possible deflection is 250 metres. That means that a certain rocket can fall 600 metres ahead of the target or 600 metres short. The possible range of error is 1.200 metres, and 50 per cent of the rockets would have to fall into an area of 600 metres by 250 meters; whereas, in actual fact in practice, the situation was much more complex. Nobody had time to measure air temperature, the force of the wind, whether the launcher was positioned exactly at the angle necessary or not, et cetera. The parameters in my report serve a different purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That was a long and somewhat technical answer. Let me see if I understood it correctly, and tell me please if I have understood it correctly. Are you saying that your estimate, which was not based on actual performances but was based on assumptions, was that the circular error probability of the FAB-250 is 600 metres by 250 metres. But you qualify that by saying that in reality with all of the different conditions, it is very hard to tell whether that is even an accurate assumption. Is that a fair characterisation of your answer that you have given us?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a small correction. CEP is the circular area; whereas, we are here dealing with the right angle. But the area where the rockets would fall is approximately equivalent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in your report, you also give very specific data regarding the accuracy of unguided rockets and artillery weapons. Can you compare, just in a sentence or two, would a FAB-250 modified air bomb be more or less accurate than an unguided rocket fired on its own or an artillery weapon fired on its own?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: FAB-250, the way it was conceived and designed and defined here, certainly has a greater dispersion than an unguided rocket that was highly professionally manufactured.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how about an artillery weapon, would it have a greater or lesser dispersion than an artillery weapon?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the artillery splash would have a greater dispersion. I showed that in my report, the data used from a study done in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So an artillery weapon would have a greater dispersion than a FAB-250 modified aircraft bomb?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Artillery weapons would have a smaller dispersion than these systems. These systems are more precise, more accurate than FAB-250.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Finally, can you compare for us please to a mortar weapon. Is a mortar weapon more or less accurate than these other weapons we have talked about; artillery weapon, unguided rocket, FAB-250?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mortars are more precise than these systems, significantly more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just to wrap up this topic, you say at page 77 of the English and 71 of the B/C/S, that based on your analysis and expertise, modified air bombs are effective only against what you call area targets. What do you mean by that, "area targets"?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'll try to say this again. In wartime conditions, when using artillery to target a small dot, a small target, or you use it at a small range, 100 metres, 200 metres, that can cover a certain area, a small area, that's when you say that you performed your technical assignment, your tactical assignment when you hit it. Other targets are fired at with hand-held rocket launchers, tank shells, or rockets.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But could you give us an example -- some examples of what are area targets? What do you have in mind when you say -- what is it, for example, on the battlefield or in a war, what is an area target, concretely?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We can look at this Russian system, TOS1. It is a modern rocket system using fuel-air explosive that is an improvement on the KREMA-4 system. It has 30 barrels, and it targets an area 200 to 400 metres -- sorry 200 by 400 metres at a range of 3.500 metres. It can destroy targets on that area. That's what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That rocket system - it is at page 89 of the English and page 80 of the B/C/S - where you talk about that particular rocket system. But I'm -- again, I think I'm asking a similar question. What kind of target is that in real life? What kind of target occupies an area like that? What are you thinking of? Can you give us a specific example what kind of target you would aim such a weapon at?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, a football pitch is 50 by 100 metres. So four times four, this would be 16 football pitches. Just to help you imagine how large the area is. At a distance of 3.500 metres, you can target 16 football pitches taken together; but you cannot hit the locker room, if you wanted to. It is impossible with this kind of system. It is possible with guided missiles, tank shells, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you move on, in the first part of your testimony, you compared the system used in Sarajevo, Sarajevo with the Russian system, and you indicated that the system used in Sarajevo was less sophisticated and therefore more inaccurate. Now, in the testimony that you have just been giving more recently, I understand that modified air bombs have a level of inaccuracy, which one might describe as inherent. So would it be correct, then, to say that the modified air bombs that we're dealing with here, at one level there is inaccuracy which resulted from less professionalism; but at another level, there is an inaccuracy which is inherent in a modified air bomb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're completely right. There are two different incident influences; the influence of design and development and the very concept of an unguided missile, which is implies the impossibility of hitting a specific individual target. If you use two systems together, that provides for greater dispersion and imprecision of these systems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to ask very briefly about another topic, and that is angle of descent. Are you able -- from the way an air bomb strikes a target, are able to determine anything about the angle of descent; that is, the angle that it came down at?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is a very important approach in determining the range of the projectile that hit the target, depending on the situation on the ground. You have to take in the whole situation on the site of the event, to identify the effects on site at the target and identify the points where the projectile first hit the target and where the explosion occurred. In a number of cases, where the projectile hit a building, one can notice the point of impact of the projectile on the building; and then inside the building, you can identify the place where the explosion occurred, because usually in that place you would find remnants of the rocket boosters; then using usual trigonometry equations, you could determine the angle of descent. That was one system. Another system applied if the projectile impacted on flat surface; then you would usually find remnants of rocket boosters embedded in ground or sand, and you could estimate, assess the angle of descent. Another factor was very important; namely, if the projectile took its effect within a neighbourhood in town, then by analysing the place of detonation and the height of the buildings over which the projectile descended, you would be able to determine the minimal angle of descent at the time of impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think we're another the break, if I could have one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, unless you're famished, we could go on for another five more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Oh, fine. Good. That's perfect, because I just have last -- one or two last questions that I had planned before the break and then some more after.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Based on your expert analysis of the aircraft bomb, and your experience, are you able to offer an opinion about whether the ABiH within Sarajevo had such a weapon during the war?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the basis of what I know, did not have similar systems because it was impossible to import rocket motors into Bosnia-Herzegovina, because they would have to go through Croatia first and then through HOV. Also, in order to have an air bomb, one had to have an explosive and the body itself. Bearing in mind how Sarajevo was being supplied through the tunnel in 1994 and 1995, then an air bomb would have to be brought down Mount Igman, and an effort would have to be made to push it through the tunnel and also manufacture other components, and that was very difficult. There was no electricity, no proper machinery; then a launching system would have to have been made. That's not simple. You see, you'd have to have trucks, guide-rails, a mechanism for azimuth, a mechanism for elevation, and so on and so forth. I am firmly convinced that there are no prerequisites for the existence of such a system within Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You made a reference in that answer -- that rather complete answer about machinery. Can you elaborate a little bit on that, that there was no machinery to accomplish this. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, in order to make an air bomb, it is necessary to have 12-millimetre steel sheets. So it has to be of high quality. You have to cut the steel, and that is done through melting; then you have to have all the right machinery for treating this steel, and then you have to have these big machines that can actually deal with an air bomb, which is of such great size and which is 325 millimetres. And we all know that in Sarajevo, there were constant power cuts at the time, and you need electricity. Also, to fill an air bomb with explosive, you need to have TNT. Every air bomb had 150 kilogrammes and more of TNT, or you have to have fuel air. People did not know about fuel air explosives in Sarajevo at the time. It was only the Vinca Institute that knew about that, the institute for atomic energy in Vinca. In order to deal with it, then you also would have to have a foundry which was in Jelsingrad; then that was under the control of the government of Republika Srpska. In order to have stabilisers, you had to have the right metal sheeting and then you had to have machines for treating stabilisers. In order to make a machine that is six metres long there -- has to be very accurate. You would have to have very big-sized machinery. That did not exist in Sarajevo. Sarajevo only had small makeshift machinery with very limited capacity of making a 120-millimetre projectile, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Last very brief question before the break. You made a reference to Vinca. Where is that, please?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Vinca is near Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think that's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll break for an hour. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.34 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm now going to move to the third area of my questioning, which is to review your analysis in chapter 17 of the specific incidents. I was going to go through all of them; but given the time, I think I'm just going to do a selection. Before I start speaking specifically or asking specifically about the incidents, I want to ask you some questions about your analysis of all of the incidents. With respect to all of the incidents that you analysed in chapter 17, were you able to reach a conclusion based on the evidence that you analysed and your expertise on what kind of weapon was used?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. The interpreters cannot here the witness. Interpreter's note: The witness should start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Please restart.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of the analysis of photographs and investigator reports on individual cases, and using the information I had and the personal insights I had with regard to individual incidents, it can be established beyond doubt that these were rocketised air bombs. And in this case, it was FAB-250s with rocket motors. Further on, in all cases, what is missing is the intensive effect of fragments at the surrounding vertical surfaces and the structure where the air bomb impacted, which shows the TNT explosive will not been used.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What kind of explosive was used then, in your determination?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The consequences that could be seen show how intensive the effect was, which beyond doubt shows that it was fuel-air explosive that was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In the cases that you analysed, were you able to determine the direction of fire and/or the origin of fire of the air bomb?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In most cases, one could assess the direction from which the projectile came and the approximate angle of descent of the projectile, and a ballistic analysis could establish the minimal range from which the objective had been targeted. In a few cases, it was necessary to compare similar cases in the area in order to reach a proper conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In the 11 cases that you analysed, that are scheduled in our indictment and that are analysed in chapter 17 of your report, can you give an opinion based on your analysis and your expertise as to whether the air bomb was fired from territory controlled by the Bosnian Serb army or territory controlled by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It has been established beyond doubt that the potential launching places were in the territory that was controlled by the army of Republika Srpska in all cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to go through some of the incidents with you. And with respect to each one, I'm essentially going to ask you three questions: I want to found out what you concluded regarding the direction of fire, the angle of descent of the air bomb, and what you then were able to conclude or approximate regarding the origin of fire. Now, if we could turn to the first one I want to ask you about, it's what we know as shelling incident number 8. It's page 117 of the English; 104 of the B/C/S. An incident that occurred on the 24th of May, 1995. Do you see that, sir? Are you on that page?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You say, on page 119 of the English and 106 of the B/C/S, that the angle was determined to be an azimuth of 155 degrees plus/minus five degrees. Who made that determination?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This conclusion was defined by the investigators. They made a sketch of the terrain, and that is where they determined the direction from where it came. That was the north. And on that basis, the incoming angle was determined, the anticipated angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, there is an angle of 20 degree, angle of descent, which is included in your report, and you conclude that the launch site was probably at a distance of 5.800 metres or more. Can you explain how that was determined in this case. What evidence did you rely on to come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I had a few approaches in defining this angle. First of all, in the photographs, it can seen clearly that the rocket motors or part of the rocket motors remained in the ground. That is already an indication of the approximate value of the angle of descent. Furthermore, in terms of the launch site, there is a hill that you can see here on this photograph, that is perhaps 400 metres away. And its altitude is a couple of hundred of metres. The altitude of that hill --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I need to interrupt you for a moment. Are you able to tell us which photograph, by referring to the page number, which photograph did you just refer to there?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Page 107. 107, the lower photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there is a number? We're on page 118?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That is on the B/C/S, and it doesn't actually have a number. But it is the photograph that appears on the top of the page on 121 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I am sorry I interrupted you, Professor. What were you saying about the hill?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This hill is of a certainly altitude, and there is a certain distance to the incident site. Ballistic analysis shows that the height of the trajectory at the point should be higher than the height or the altitude of the hills, so that the projectile could reach the incident site; and that is why, on the basis of this analysis, I said that an angle of 20 degrees of launching would be the minimum one for the projectile to be able to fly over the hill. However, now, if we look at the broader area of this minimal distance, I suggested that it was more likely that the launching angle is about 5.000 metres or more, because it would be more desirable for the launching site to be outside the urban area, which was then under the control of the army of Republika Srpska. These are quite clear criteria that the -- if the angle were less than 20 degree, it is would not fly over the hill and it could not land in the street of the Safeta Zajke. So the minimum range is 4.800 metres. The probable launch range is 5.800 metres or even more. In both case, the launch site is under the control of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you are -- once you are able to determine an angle of descent based offer pieces of evidence, from that are you able to determine a minimum or maximum range? Is there any connection between those two things?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The minimal range can be established, and the maximum rage is defined by the performance of the rocket system. So the approximate or probable area where the launcher was can be established.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's look at the next incident. It's incident number 9 for us, and it's on page 122 of the English and 109 of the B/C/S. With respect to this incident, were you able to come to any conclusions regarding the direction of fire and the range.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the investigators' reports, the direction was defined. It was not possible to establish the incoming angle of the projectile. However, when one looks at the distance in the previous case and in this case, and if we take as a point of departure that both incidents occurred the same day within four hours or so, then, bearing in mind the fact that this same hill is behind the incident site, it is only logical that the launching sites in both cases are similar; and then it was possible to proceed from the assumption that the direction was identical as in the previous case, and also the incoming angle would have to be at a minimum 20 degrees in order to be able to hit this particular site. So, the location for the launcher in this case has to be at a minimum range of 4.800 metres; that is to say, that the distance from this incident, and that site would then be within the broader area of Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could look now at incident number 12, which is at page 132 of the English and 118 of the B/C/S. On page 133 of the English, and I'm not sure which page of the B/C/S, if it's 118 or 119, you say that the azimuth angle of 285 degrees was determined. Can you tell us how that was determined, and if you able in this incident to determine a range of how far away it was fired from?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You see that what I said here was that this analysis was possible only after a detailed analysis of other locations where buildings had been hit the area of Novo Sarajevo; that is to say, in the immediate neighbourhood. The projectile fell on a small flat area behind an apartment building. So, in order to have the projectile hit that area, it had to go by that apartment building, which is an eight story building of 20-odd metre. So the difference is, say, about 20 metres between the point of impact and the top of the building. And if we look at the distance from the site of this incident and the vertical surface of the building, it is possible to establish what the minimal angle was. And if we were to compare this to similar incidents that occurred in the area, it was possible to establish the area from where the -- it had been launched; 75 degrees to the west, or rather, 285 degrees azimuth. On my photograph on page 119, it is the next one, the next photograph, the next page of this particular incident. And you can see there these red and white dots.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So the photograph you're referring to is on our page 134 at the top. When I say "our page," I mean the English. Were you able, based on your calculation of the angle of descent, to determine the -- an approximate range from which this was fired?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Around 5.8 kilometres. That is the broader area of Butile. However, I have to say that the position depends on the roads there. A launcher is mounted on a truck so probably it had to take a proper road to that particular site. It is not possible for that truck to go through inaccessible areas; that is to say, communication has to be possible when one looks at the launching. You see many red and white dots here showing the grouping of hits in the narrow area of the city of Sarajevo. That is how I established what the possible position was, a bit more accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now you -- I think you've already said that with respect range you would come up with an approximation, a -- a minimum and a maximum, for example. With respect to direction of fire, based on your analysis, was it possible to come up with a precise determination or an approximate determination of the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In most cases it was possible to have a relative degree of accuracy, plus/minus five per cent, to assess what the azimuth was. It was impossible to assess it to a single degree. That is impossible, but it was possible to establish what the -- or, rather, assess the corridor that the projectile could have taken in order to get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. Can we look now at shelling incident 13, which is at page 135 of the English; page 121 of the B/C/S. And here you describe how the reports from the investigators have a conflict in terms of the direction of fire. Some of the reports say north-west and there's -- I believe one report that says north-east. Were you able to come to a conclusion based on your analysis of what the direction of fire was for this incident?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I carried out a full analysis of the area of the incident, not only relying on the photographs in the investigator reports but by carrying out an on-site visit and analysing the entire region in 3D form in order to be able to assess it. That was my foundation for establishing the minimum angle of descent. I defined the point of impact, where the projectile impacted the building. Then, across -- or, rather opposite that building there is an apartment building that is about 12 metres higher than the point of impact and the distance is about 25 metres, and in that way it was possible to establish the minimal angle of descent. The projectile would have hit that building had the angle been smaller. Once I determined this minimum angle of descent on the basis of a ballistic analysis proceeding from the original data of the investigators, I saw that it was impossible to launch the projectile from the north or some other direction because at a distance of 5200 metres, that is the distance involved and determined by the angle of launching, it is possible to establish that this area is very hilly. So in order to be able to fly over these hills, its trajectory would have to be considerably higher than the 5800 that I referred to. Since I'm familiar with the area, it is in the area of the Pretis factory where I worked for about 20 years. The only broader location where it was -- from where it was possible to carry out the launching and to have a clear area of several hundred metres in front of the launching pad without hitting an obstacle was the interior area of the Pretis factory or, rather, the area right next to the entrance into the Pretis factory. Anything else would have made the launching of the projectile impossible. So that was the reason that made it possible for me to assess the azimuth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's move now to shelling incident 15. It's at page 140 of the English and 125 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And this is the incident involving the TV tower.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now you testified early that you participated in the investigation of this incident at the time. What was your role?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I did not take part in the investigation. I carried out - how should I put this? - an independent case, independently of the judge, Judge Bazdarevic, together with two of my colleagues who are ballistics men. One is a ballistics expert and the other one is an explosives expert. We analysed this incident, and since, on the same day, several incidents occurred in the immediate vicinity of the TV tower we carried out an analysis and we compiled our own report that we handed over to the judge. So, in a way, we were an independent commission apart from the police, that is. Separate from the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you do -- did you undertake this investigation on your own or were you asked by somebody to do it?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. Right after the firing of this projectile at the TV tower, the judge telephoned me and asked me to come and carry out an analysis. I have his decision on the investigation too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you go to the scene on that day. On the day that it occurred, did you go to the TV tower?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very quickly. Perhaps within an hour or an hour and a half after the impact, I was on site.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And so if it occurred -- you have it occurring at 9.22. You believe you were there by 10.30 or 11.00?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, there is a matter that has been troubling me. The witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Isn't this witness testifying as an expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes. But this -- he was, I would submit, asked as an expert to analyse this incident, and so his analysis of the incident that occurred at the time figures into his expert analysis today in his report about the incident. So that is why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where is his expertise in this area set out?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In -- I'm sorry, in which area? In terms of investigating incidents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. Investigating --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The use of modified aircraft bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, his expertise is set out in -- in the first chapter. His experience in dealing with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's on page 1, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Hang on. Yes, page 1. And I'm happy to elaborate on it further. I thought this was not a matter of dispute. That based on his experience at the Pretis factory plus teaching experience plus his experience during the war, he has developed an expertise in -- in artillery rocket launching and this kind of weaponry. And this experience extends -- his primary field of work was rocket motors and warheads, developing rocket projectiles. He has experience both in terms of developing the weapons and understanding and knowing the characteristics of the weapons, but also understanding how they impact on targets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you have not demonstrated how he acquired that experience. And, indeed, on page 1, which is headed "Personal Qualifications and Professional Experience," it is more devoted to professional experience than his qualifications. You have described him as a professor, but we don't know how he reached that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I certainly have to ask some more questions about that. I thought I had done sufficient on this, but obviously I haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I don't think you have. I don't think whether the Defence had intended to take it up, but what is here doesn't really establish his expertise, in my view. Although, it is clear from the evidence that he has been giving that he does have a fairly deep knowledge of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Professor, you've, I think, heard the intervention of the Trial Chamber. Could you assist us please, and I'll put the question generally first and then may ask some detailed follow-up. Could you assist in explaining to us what expertise you have, based both on -- and you can rely both on your learning and your teaching, your practical experience, working at the Pretis factory, and also practical experience during the war in two subjects: First, the characteristics and qualities of aircraft bombs and modified aircraft bombs with rockets. And, number two, assessing or analysing impact of those bombs and making analysis, such as you have, about what type of bomb, what type of weapon, where it came from. What qualifications do you have to do those two tasks which you do in your report.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In 1975, I completed -- I graduated from the Faculty of Mechanical Engineering. The topic of my diploma paper was design of 128-millimetre descent rockets. That same year I got employment in Pretis in the development department, and I worked on the development of that rocket, which over a period of years was further developed and became part of the weaponry of the JNA, and it came to be known as 128-millimetre M87. So I developed a new rocket motor, a new warhead, complete analysis of external and internal design. I tested more than 2.000 rockets in flight and more than 700 rocket motors during the testing stage. At the same time, I taught at the Mechanical Engineering Faculty in the department for me are mechanics, first; and then when the department for defence was formed at the university, I taught in that department. So from 1984, I'm -- I teach in the department for ammunitions, rocket motors, testing of those. I later got a diploma in Zagreb in the area of pyrotechnology, internal ballistics of rocket motors, which fly at very high speeds, to simplify things. In 1999, I took a Ph.D. At the Mechanical Engineering Faculty in Sarajevo. My thesis was on the combustion of rocket fuel in the area of high angle velocity, which is a topic directly linked to these rockets. By working in Pretis, I also worked on the 128-millimetre rockets and artillery projectiles of 122-millimetres mortar shells of 120 millimetres. Just before the war, I developed the improved rocket of 122-millimetres with a range of 27 kilometres and one of 36 kilometres for the needs of the Egyptian military industry. I developed the rocket of 50-millimetres as a test rocket for testing large rocket -- armoured rocket systems. I developed the 90-millimetre rockets for combat in case of assault. And during the war, in 1992 and 1993, we tried to find alternative ways of manufacturing ammunitions within available resources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. You are a professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a head of the department for defensive weapons at the Faculty of Mechanical Engineering. I have four assistants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm just going to follow-up with a few questions. In your capacity as a professor, have you published any articles.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't be appointed to the post of professor if I hadn't published such articles. I have published and participated in a large number of international congress and symposia. In 1980, I was awarded, together with a colleague, Nenad Fisher, in Tokyo as the best paper on the combustion of fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell us, in addition to that paper, just briefly, some of the other topics that have you published on that might be relevant to your analysis in this case.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I published articles in the areas of the combustion of rocket motors, their design and fragmentation of warheads, definition of the zone of lethal affect, when a projectile contacts the target; then also I published some papers on uranium. I published the effect of the shelling of the old bridge in Mostar. I was president of the commission for establishing the position of the launcher for Markale 1. I did an analysis of that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just to follow-up on that particular point, have you ever testified as an expert before at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I am sorry. The interpreters didn't hear that. Could please you repeat that answer please.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did testify I think I did testify in the Galic case as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That was on what issue, if you can recall? What did you testify about in the Galic case?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I testified in evaluating the possible positions from which the 120-millimetre mortar shell was launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Which mortar shell? Was it in respect to a particular incident?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 120-millimetre in the Markale incident, Markale 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then the final question, not to overdo this but just to be complete. You testified about having participated in or been involved in many tests of weapons. I think, you said 2.000, but some large numbers of tests of weapons of rockets. Did those tests include in addition to the flight of the weapon, the impact of the weapon? In other words, have you studied that, the impact ever weapons, such as rockets on targets?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Fully. I designed a rocket system as a whole. For it to be included in the weaponry of the JNA, it had to be fully tested; the rocket motors, the warheads, the ballistics, the reliability, the fragmentation tables of the targeting, and a whole series of other things. I worked in this area continuously for a period of ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thank you for allowing me to develop the record on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could go back to shelling incident 15, page 140 of the English, 125 of the B/C/S, and you were testifying that you went to the scene at -- I think you said 10.30 or 11.00 that day. When you arrived at the scene, were other -- were there other investigators already at the scene, or were you the first to arrive at the scene?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. I wasn't the first to arrive. There were the police officers who were there, and they were to assist me in taking photographs, and they went to this area together with me, so I wasn't alone. There was a three-man team working on this analysis, and we reached the original place of contact of the projectile with the TV building and then we analysed the other elements and examined how such a destructive effect could have been achieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: As part of your analysis in this case, have you reviewed photographs of the destruction caused by the air bomb on that day, on the TV tower?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I toured all the different parts of the building, every part that was damaged. And during the analysis in preparing this report, I did review those photographs and they fully correspond to what I personally saw with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You anticipated my question. Thank you. Did you -- oh, by the way, did you -- do you recall if you saw any UNMOs present at the scene when you were there?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I did not notice any just then, because just after I arrived and made the first tour of the area, another projectile hit close to the TV and then I went to examine that and then there was another incident in the Geteova Street. So I went to tour all these sites to have a fuller insight and it's quite possible, while I was absent, that some of them or one of them may have arrived, but I don't remember. I don't remember meeting them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long were you at the TV tower site, after you arrived?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the late afternoon about 5.00 p.m., I received a photograph of the launcher --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- published by the journal, Europa.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think you misunderstood. You testified that you went to the site at approximately 10.30 or 11.00. How long did you remain there? How long were you there, at the TV tower, before you left?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When I had visited these different locations, this may have taken 15 or 20 minutes, I spent the rest of the time, until 5.00 p.m., there at the TV tower.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said in answer to Mr. Whiting's question that on that day he saw a photograph in the magazine Europa, and this was not included in the transcript. It just says "magazine," but what the witness said is not included in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That he saw the photograph in the magazine, Europa?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, your intervention has included it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you write a report on the basis of your investigation?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After about seven or ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you reach a conclusion about what type of bomb was used in that incident?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my conclusion was that it was an aerosol bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was your report, your conclusion, accepted?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, it was not accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know why not, did you learn why not?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just before handing in my report, a meeting was organised in the Defence Ministry because one of the members of the commission was a member of the Defence Ministry in the section for the military industry and his boss asked us to come to a meeting and two officers were present there from the Security Service of the Main Staff. At the time they insisted that we change our conclusion to the effect that it was not an aerosol bomb but a different bomb, a bomb with TNT. I rejected this initiative and it was a bit unpleasant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a few questions about this. First of all, who insisted that you change your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Two men who introduced themselves as being from the intelligence or counter-intelligence service of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did they tell you or did you learn why it was they wanted you to change your conclusion -- that it was -- and change it from being --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Asked them, because their impression was that it would be more effective if it was stated that the explosive used was TNT. I think that they weren't sufficiently informed about the effects of fuel-air bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you say that your impression was that it would be more effective, what do you mean by that? More effective in what way? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know how to explain it. Probably in their minds, they felt that if it said an air bomb with TNT, then possible consequences of destruction are greater than if it is stated that it was a fuel air bomb. It was not so frequently used, in daily use.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that it became unpleasant. In what way did it become unpleasant? Can you be more specific about that?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At a point in time, they started threatening me that they would send me to prison if I did not change my conclusion. However, as this was not the first instance from my opinion to differ from the opinion of military leaders at the time or members of the Defence Ministry, I did not agree to their suggestion, and I stood by my position. The other two members of the commission, I must point out, supported me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you did not change your report?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Does this episode that you experienced cause you to doubt any of the police or investigator reports that you have reviewed in connection with the incidents that you have analysed in your report?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
