utterances.text: No. The reports are very correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to the incident that you analysed. You determined that the incoming direction was 280 degrees, that the angle of descent was 25 degrees, and therefore the minimum distance was 5.800 metres for the launch. Could you very briefly, because we're short on time, explain to us what it was that caused you to reach this conclusion. What did you base that conclusion on?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The most important proof are the prints of the impact of the bomb on the roof of this tower. One can clearly see an elongated imprint with deep deformations of the ground, and one can also see that the damage is a couple of metres long and the depth about 200 millimetres, on the basis of classical systems of the evaluation of effects of targets, which is defined by American rules. Also, on projectiles, it was possible with precision of plus/minus ten to determine the direction of fire. As the prints were very intensive, it meant that the penetration angle was about 25 degrees, the ricochet angle. And this could be clearly be seen, the bomb hit the roof, it ricochetted, and fell into this area between the studio. And that is it where destruction of the -- part of the casing occurred, the activation of the explosive, the activation of secondary fuses, and the destruction that is it evidenced on these photographs. As I knew the direction --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going interrupt you, I'm sorry, because I think you have answered the question. But one more question on this incident. Based on the evidence that you reviewed and that you have just described, is it possible that the air bomb -- this air bomb was fired from a distance of less than 1.000 metres away? Is that possible, given the physical evidence that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I shall explain that very simply.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: First answer, and then can you briefly explain?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, it is not possible. It is not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now briefly explain, please.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You see, an air bomb is supplied with three rocket motors. Their time is between 1.6 to 2 seconds, so the maximum speed is about 250 metres per second at the end of the work of the rocket motor. So a rocket projectile has an active period. The trajectory, while the motor is functioning, is 400 metres. There is no possibility of that rocket, once the motor stops working, being able to change its course and have an angle of 25 degrees. It is simple. The system has its own inertia. You must not forget that 250 metres per second is in the range of 800 kilometres per hour or 500 miles per hour. This is a very high speed, and the mass is about 300 kilograms. That is the mass weight of the bomb, so it is impossible to guide such a system to make sudden turns.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, finally, I'm just going to ask you to look quickly at one last incident. It's what we call shelling incident 19, and it's at page 150 of the English and 135 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, before you move on to that, I must admit that I'm not sure I fully understand the explanation that the witness just gave to the reason why the TV bomb could not have been fired from a distance less than 1.000 metres. If I look at the transcript, the witness, Professor, you said that the time is between 1.6 to 2 seconds, so that the maximum speed is about 250 metres per second. What time are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The time that the rocket motor is working, while the fuel is burning. Once there is no further burning of feel, the projectile continues along its route by inertia. It doesn't have its own inertia, so a great force is required to turn it around. So the Prosecutor was asking me whether it was possible to hit the TV tower from a distance of 1.000 metres. I'm saying, at this position, if you're targeting from a distance of one kilometre, the traces would not be what they were here. There is no possibility of the rocket changing its course and ricochetting on the roof of the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What I understand you to say is that if the angle of descent was about 20 degrees, then it must have been fired from a longer distance, provided, I understand, provided that the rockets were functioning all the time. But a natural question would be: What happens if the rocket motor suddenly fails so that the bomb is just launched and then after one or two or three seconds, there is no more propulsion so then it drops. Would that be a possibility? Could that have happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible for the rocket motor to fail. It is possible, but then the rocket will not continue to fly in that direction. It will move to the right, to the left, upwards or downwards. It cannot continue its flight in the direction it started in, because there is destabilisation. There are three rocket motors and the vector of propulsion must be parallel. Should one rocket motor fail, then there is destabilisation, and it will fall towards the ground after 100 metres. There is to dilemma in that regard. This is a well-known fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just follow-up with a question here. So if the bomb were to keep its trajectory under a failure of the rockets, then that would require that all three rockets stopped at exactly the same time. Is that correct? Which, in my view, would be unlikely, but that could be a possibility.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The motors cannot fail. They can only explode. The whole system is so designed. For a rocket to leave the launcher, it must have a minimum speed of 50 metres per second. So in the first stage, the rocket motors must be working properly or the projectile will not leave the launcher. If the velocity is reduced business because the motors are not producing the necessary propulsion, then the rocket is no longer stable, because we designed the size of the stabiliser of the rocket according to the maximum speed indicated by the motor. If the speed is lower in the launching stage, then the stabiliser surface has to be larger. That is a principle of dynamics and ballistics. If the propulsion by three motors were inadequate, it couldn't fly in a stable manner. It would fall again. It would drop. It cannot fly regularly. It is very simple for people in this field of aerodynamics and ballistics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can't the failure occur at 1.000 metres in the same way it could occur at 100?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It cannot at 1.000 metres because a rocket motor works for only 1.6 to 2 seconds. It is working for the first 400 metres only; after that, the rocket motors are not working any longer and so any failure has no effect after that. It has already acquired its velocity, stability, and inertia. And the system works notice same way as if you were to throw a stone from your shoulder. It's unguidable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Just to clarify again, the time that mentioned in your first intervention, 1.6 to 2 seconds, that is the time when the rockets are ignited and working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And during those 1.6 to 2 seconds, the bomb would have moved approximately, was it, 400 metres; and from there on, the rest of the trajectory is ballistic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Freely. Free flight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I will just ask one follow-up question on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If the air bomb -- you said that if it had been launched from a closer distance, say, under 100 metre, it is would have resulted in different traces on the building. Can you -- how would they have been different? What way would it be different, the trace on the building, if it had been launched from a closer distance, say, under 1.000 metres?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In that case, the bomb would graze -- in order to reach -- if it were to reach the roof at smaller angles, it would graze the flat surface of the roof, and there would be no such intense deformations as created at an angle of 25 degrees. From an analysis of vector of inertia forces and analysis of the reaction, we can establish that. At smaller angles, therefore, there would be just mild traces on the surface of the roof. There would be no damage up to 200 millimetres deep into the roof, and there would be no such trail. 200 millimetres is written, not 2.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I think you did say 200 millimetres. Right. If we could move on to shelling incident number 19, the last one I will ask you about. Again, it's at page 150 of the English and 135 of the B/C/S. Now, in this case, the investigators concluded that there was one air bomb that ricochetted and hit two locations; however, you have come to a different conclusion. Can you just explain why it was that you came to a different conclusion with respect to this incident, and what your conclusion was?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My conclusion was there existed two air bombs that within a relatively short space of time hit two spots that were close to each other. In the first case, with regard to Aleksa Santic 50 building, the bomb hit the corner of the building, penetrated and caused extensive damage, hit the ground in the yard; and inside, deep in the ground, remnants of the rocket booster were found. From analysing the point of impact on the building and the spot where the remnants of the rocket motor were found, it was possible to calculate both the direction of descent and the angle of descent. In the case of the second building, at Bunicki Potok 233, where there was an explosion causing extensive damage due to the blastwave, I placed both these incidents on the map. I located them on the map, and I concluded that these were two separate cases and that the report saying that the rocket, after hitting the ground, deviated by 90 degrees and hit Bunicki Potok is absolutely not authenticate. First, because it's impossible to manipulate an unguided projectile go, and second, the degree was too high. The radius in such cases has to be several hundred metres. That's one thing. And the second [as interpreted] thing, it is the bomb that contacts first, that impacts first, and only then rocket motors. It isn't logical that rocket motors are grounded and the warhead which has a larger mass should be found ahead of it. The following is a rough draft which should be proofed. I interviewed witnesses in both these cases, once I noticed this inconsistency, and with the witness who lives just across the street I -- speaking to this lady, I heard that the bomb hit the man-hole of the water-supply system that some sort of grey fog dispersed after impact, and that is difficult for fuel-air explosive. Plus, and we can see this on photographs, the whole area was soaked in water, and the effect of the fuel-air explosive was compromised, because the fuel-air mixed with water. That was the first case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask you a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There's a technical problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yeah, there seems to be a technical problem. I don't know if we can continue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No transcript or no LiveNote? The technicians are on their way. Well, let's give them a couple of minutes. We'll stay here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We're just having a problem with the transcript, Professor. --- Break taken at 2.36 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Professor, just staying with this incident number 19 and the two -- what you found to be two air bombs, were you able, based on the evidence, to determine the direction of fire of the two air bombs?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The direction of descent and the angle of descent I could determine with great precision and I -- you can see that from the photographs attached.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. That's the -- okay. So the -- when you say the direction of descent, is that the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So you were able to determine both the direction of fire and the angle of descent. Was the direction of fire that you determined consistent with the direction of fire that was found by the investigators who investigated this incident and who found that there was one air bomb?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In principle, yes. One should bear in mind that the incident occurred late at night and the investigators arrived on the next day. It was said the projectile had come from the direction of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, based on the information that you analysed and your determination of the angle of descent, were you able to determine an approximate range from which it was fired from?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That can be very easily seen. That angle is around 25 degrees and the distance is 5.000 metres, or thereabouts. 5800 was the distance normally at a degree of 25 --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to the other incidents that I did not ask you about, that we did not look at in detail, did you rely on similar factors in reaching your conclusions about angle of descent, direction of fire, and the range from which the weapon was fired. That is, the topography, the photographs, the information about the damage?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I'm Defence counsel for Mr. Dragomir Milosevic, and I have quite a few questions concerning your expertise and your report. But just so I don't forget, since you were just talking about an angle of 25 degrees and the distances you established on that basis, if I'm not mistaken you always proceeded from that angle, 25 degrees, and you determined always the greatest distances for the firing of these rockets. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. If you -- you might have noticed that I also spoke about an angle of 20 degrees as well as an angle of 25 degrees. Concerning certain matters I said that the angle can be 30 or more degrees if you look at individual incidents. For each of these angles I gave a mathematical interpretation to explain how I determined that angle, so I cannot give you a general answer unless you ask me about a specific incident and ask if I had a different approach in determining the angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will have to come back to that later but I wanted to pick it up immediately and emphasise it. We are talking here about an imperfect system, and my question is, if that system is so imperfect, how come that we are dealing with these approximate values, 20, 25 degrees, and it always turns out, according to your calculations, that it was fired from four to five kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If you listen carefully, I never said that the distance from which the projectile was fired was 5.000. I said always the minimum distance was, and then it could be 800, 1.000 metres, and so on. I also spoke about the dispersion -- impact deviation, and how it can be affected by changes in temperature by change of pressure impulse and other influences. If you launch a similar projectile while changing the temperature or the rocket booster, the mass, or if there is a wind, there can be differences in range of 500 to 600 metes. You need to know this. I would be deluding you if I said, as a serious person, that the distance was 5.800 metres. I was always talking about minimum and maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I understood that. You did speak of these things in responding to the questions of the Prosecutor. I am ask you something different. This is deviation possible with every projectile, both guided and unguided. This deviation is always the limit of maximum range, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand you. Impact deviation is possible at any distance from the place of launching. The character of deviation depends on the angle of launching. That is strictly controlled, because we are talking about differences in metres when we speak of guided missiles. And with unguided missiles, the differences are measured in dozens of metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me come to page 184 of the English version of your report, where you said that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina did not have or use this type of modified aircraft bomb anywhere during the war and certainly not in Sarajevo. Could you tell me, first, before I ask you anything else - and that's also contained in your report - you had at your disposal information that this weapon had been used both in 1994 and in 1995 throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you just define when I had that information? Now, when I made my analysis, or during the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to that. For the time being, I'm on this page of your report, and it would take me time to move to another passage. You have that report in front of you. Could you please look to the end of that page. You say that the BH army did not have or use this type of modified aircraft bomb anywhere during the war. Now I'm speaking primarily, and only in fact, about the BH army, that it didn't have this weapon, right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: According to my information, and this is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You also said here something that you repeated in answering the questions of the Prosecutor, that you could not make that weapon because you lacked the sheets, you lacked the fuses, you lacked the conditions for manufacturing this weapon. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You're talking to me as if I was the one manufacturing it. I had no opportunity to be involved in manufacturing this. If you are identifying me with the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I think you're wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I did hear that, and don't personalise the questions in that way. There is no basis for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, then I will have to proceed slowly and start putting to the witness certain evidence that I have in approximate my hands, and I will start with the document DD00-1985. That's the statement given by Mr. Berko Zecevic on the 26th and 27th February, 1996 to the OTP investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see that statement? Is it your statement?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Probably. I can't see my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Look at page 2. To avoid as personalising anything here - and I usually try to avoid that - on page 2, in paragraph 2, you said: "As a member of the expert team, at the beginning of the war, I organised the production and development of weapons in Sarajevo." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So why would it be impossible for to you have been involved in the production of air bombs?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you could hear and read it that when the war began, I was a legal citizen of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; and as a legal citizen, I placed my services in the defence of the country called Bosnia and Herzegovina when the war began, and I gave all I could. Before that, I worked for 20 years in the production of weapons until 1993; and on 14th February, 1993, I was demobilised as an unsuitable person from the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you worked on the production of these weapons in cooperation with the staff of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was head of the department for development. And as head of department, I was deputy commander for the centre of production, and that was directly under the control of the staff of the Main Staff of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'll have to go back to that at some point, but I now I would like to move on to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, first of all, could this document be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, this is an interview that is nine pages long, and counsel has just put to him one sentence which he did not dispute and was actually something that he talked about in the direct. I'm not sure why the whole document then suddenly comes into evidence. On what basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to explain this. If I have enough time, from that document, I will use all of three pages, in excerpts, very important things related to the this witness. I'm not going to stick to that only. I have to link it up with yet another statement, and two other statements. All of them are his statements, that is why I am cross-examining. That is what I'm entitled to ask on cross-examination. The Prosecutor cannot tell me how I am going to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D170, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like us to have a look at this other statement. This is a conversation that Mr. Berko Zecevic had with Prosecutor Chester Stamp on the 21st and 22nd of June 2001. The document is DD00-2035.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. Just a little technical matter, which may or may not be important. This is not a statement, as we normally use that term in, in the sense that it was not signed and adopted by the witness. It is notes of an interview. With that clarification, I certainly have no objection to counsel using it in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, he said statement, first, and then he said a conversation. So let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, first of all, I'm interested in the fourth paragraph. In English, it is page -- or rather, the last paragraph. "When you're talking about the manufacturing of shells, the shells produced in Sarajevo were not made of raw steel but from pieces of steel or cast steel." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Not to dwell on this much longer, in the last paragraph on that page, page 2, paragraph 3 in English. The shells --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt but I don't believe the witness has -- I think the witness is the only one in the courtroom who does not have a copy of this in front of him. I may be mistaken, but what is on the screen is not this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Well, let the witness have a copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's on the screen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The witness has it on the screen, and I have it in my hands, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So since we've dealt with that, in the last paragraph: "Shells in Sarajevo were made in the Alipasino Polje foundry. They were mostly 82-millimetres for the most part."

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part. But a moment ago, you said that shells of 120-millimetre were made, too?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the mortar shells, yes, 120 millimetres, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I would like to tender this document as well. I would like to have it admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But not at Livnica, in Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It is your statement. It is what you said in this interview.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What was said in my interview was that at Alipasino Polje, which is a broad area, there is a factory called Livnica. In this Livnica foundry, there were cast components that were made. And I said that morning that the maximum calibre that could have been made within Sarajevo was 120 millimetres, right? I am very specific when I talk. And also if you look at this here, you will see that certain projectiles were made with a full profile. It says here made with pieces of steel; and then a complex technology makes it possible to make projectiles of 120 millimetres. But all this requires energy, electricity, tools, machinery, and so on and so forth, and you must admit that things were very complex in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, even if was complex, you manufactured that.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I did not. Please. We are not two different sides. Bosnia and Herzegovina is one state. That is the only state that exists. Within Bosnia-Herzegovina, there is not a we, you, and us. Please. I want my integrity to be protected. You keep repeating this. Sorry. I'm a professional. And very professionally, I treated everyone here whenever I came here very professionally. I was not engaged there ethnic divisions, and I do not allow for that kind of thing. I am an anti-ethnic person. I am an a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I approach every human being as a human being.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what I have done? What is it that I have done?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't won't any overlapping, and the witness should compose himself and we'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. Though, Your Honour, I would object that counsel did, once again, say "you" were manufacturing shells at that location, and counsel has been warned about that. That is, in my submission, what provoked the witness, so I don't think that particularly is fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I warned you about that. I don't see any basis for putting to the witness questions beginning, "you," as though he is the alter ego of either the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the ABiH army. So just reformulate your questions, and let us avoid that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I also, Your Honour, it got a little lost. I make the same objection with respect to the admission of this report, just for the purposes of this record. Counsel offered it into evidence. I make the same objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't understand your objection. It is an interview in which he was involved, and he has not denied it. He has offered a clarification in respect of part of its contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my submission, there are rules about when prior interviews of a witness come into evidence. They -- it is either under 92 bis or 92 ter or under -- because in cross-examination, it contains something that contradicts what the witness has said. None of those requirements have been met here. It doesn't seem to me that there is a basis in the rules, and certainly there is no basis in my common law background for -- for prior interviews to just come in wholesale like this. He reads one sentence of it, and then the whole interview comes in. So that is the basis of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll admit it. We'll take the break now. But before we do, I am to say that the Chamber orders that the photographs taken during the site visit to Sarajevo, 19th March to the 22nd, be admitted into evidence. We'll break. 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm compelled to repeat what I had asked the witness first, as I put his statement to him. That is why I used the word "you." The witness confirmed that, as a member of the expert team at the beginning of the war in Sarajevo, he organised the production and development of weaponry, and that he did that in cooperation with the staff of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So when I said "you" to him, Your Honours, I didn't really say anything else but what he himself had confirmed. He wasn't working for himself. He was working for the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I think in that situation, in that context, it is permissible because he is referring to your statement. So please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I answered the question, that I organised the process of production in 1992 and 1993 for the needs of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo. I have already given a clear answer to that. That was yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That is why I am saying "you" in my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm forced to hurry with these documents, and I will now just go back to one of them in greater detail. Now, again, I would like to see another document, DD00-2001. Again, this is an interview that Mr. Berko Zecevic had with a representative of the OTP, John Tate-Harris, a very important thing attachment. Could we please look at page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're waiting on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here it is. Look at the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say here that you worked on experiments regarding the 120-millimetre shell; and then under 3, you say: "With regard to the whistling sound made by mortars," the witness stated that he was aware of it before the war, but took little notice of it, as is it did not form a relative part of his scientific war. During the war, Zecevic paid great attention to the noise a mortar makes. As he stated, it gave one enough time to run for cover. To listen to the noise could save one's life. Is that the characteristic of the 120-millimetre mortar shell? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The characteristic of all rotating projectiles that move through the air. So it doesn't have anything to do with the 120-millimetre mortar. That is the characteristic. It depends on a great many factors, the intensity of sound. So whether you hear it or not, depends on where you are, whether there is a building in front of you or not. So this is a question of principle, and I gave an answer of principle. As for specific answers, we can talk about that because there are pros and cons involved. Sorry. That is why it says here that it is possible for some to hear it. I'm not saying that everyone can hear it. I'm just saying that there is a chance of a person saving his or her life.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: However, can we say that such a sound cannot be -- or rather, the most precise apparatus and equipment for registering sound cannot miss it?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What equipment?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The Cymbelline, for instance.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's radar based, and that is quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to insist on this any longer. You have given your answer, and what I am interested in is contained in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could this document please be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will admit this as D172. Also, the previous document, DD00-0235, will go in as D171.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Finally, I would like to go back to the first document too, the witness statement that he gave on the 20th and 21st of July, 1992, and that is document DD00-1960. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I can't see it on my screen yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You signed it?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My signature can be seen here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is such that I would like to look at a big paragraph from page 10 in, B/C/S, and in the English version it is page 10 as well, paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is what you say here, the paragraph that says: "From April/May 1993." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I still cannot see it. Where does it say April/May? On the right-hand side, I cannot see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the third paragraph. It has to be lowered a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "From April/May 1993, mortar shells and projectiles fired on Sarajevo by the Serbian forces were manufactured in Serbia." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It's your statement.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "I know that as from August 1992, I introduced a practice of collecting," - that is to say, you did - "unexploded ordnances, mines, projectiles to use explosives extracted from them for the BiH government forces." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "I would ask volunteers to go around Sarajevo and collect these unexploded ordnances." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "This is a practice that in normal situations should not be under taken; but as the government forces were seriously short of weapons, there was no alternative." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "From each kilogram of explosives I could extract from the ordnance, one could manufacture ten rifle grenades." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "As was the usual practice in Yugoslavia, the ordnances people brought into me had the year and place of manufacture." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you made not only rifle grenades - I have to say "you" because you organised the making of these rifle grenades, as you said a few moments ago - also of shells of 82-millimetre calibre and 120-millimetre calibre?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Not correct. Because I was head of the R&D department; the research and development department of military products, that is. This was a unit that was attached to the Main Staff. At the same time, there was the Pretis factory, a parallel factory without the machinery, as opposed to the one in Vogosca. They worked on the production of projectiles for mortars. So the unit that was in, in 1992, had the primary task of creating prerequisites for normalising the process of producing ammunitions, which was taken over by Pretis, that I had no contact with. So my unit, up to the moment when it was disbanded in June 1993, primarily did -- manufactured ammunitions for rifle grenades. These were projectiles fired off a rifle, and hand grenades, too. We did not make mortar shells of 82 millimetres; that is to say, where I personally participated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But others did?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me where the Pretis factory was that was manufacturing these shells?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This was, as you know, the government of the Republika Srpska and the government of the HOV and the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, once the war started, created a brother factories. There was a Pretis in Vogosca, a Pretis in Sarajevo, and Pretis in Sarajevo [as interpreted]. So you had a series of other companies, and each side expected that it would take control, because the Pretis company had a great deal of debts from Iraq measured in hundreds of millions of dollars, and that is why everyone wanted to the keep the name Pretis, in order to be able to collect those dues. It is very complicated but that is how it was. Therefore, Pretis was a fictitious name, which used the facilities of other companies, or event the facilities of private individuals, for the manufacture of various ammunitions. It didn't have its own plants or facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When talking about unexploded ordnance or shells that were found and that had markings on them as being manufactured in Serbia, you endeavoured, when making rifle grenades, to retain those markings as if they had been manufactured in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. There is no possibility of launching with a piece of artillery, any artillery projectile that had already been fired from another weapon. What I wrote here means that I was responsible for establishing the process of production under impossible conditions. As there was a shortage of explosives, I demanded that all artillery and mortar shells that are unexploded be brought to me, and then I organised the extraction of the explosives. And you will see that for every kilogram of explosive taken from such a weapon, we could manufacture ten rifle grenades. So try and compare it. If somebody hit at you with a projectile and it doesn't explode, and my men find them and they extract the explosive from it, 2.6 kilograms of explosives, at risk of life, and the Howitzer projectiles, for instance, can have a range of ten to 15 kilometres, my response is up to 300 metres. So let us not mislead each other by making a comparison. This was just an attempt to obtain explosives. Collecting artillery projectiles was designed simply to extract explosives from it. There was no other element involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the document 1960 be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D173, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, you said that these air bombs could not be manufactured - not that you couldn't manufactured them. I apologise - but that they couldn't be manufactured because there was a shortage of steel. And among other reasons, there is was no fuses. That is what it says in your statement here.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A fuses, sheets for stabilisers, electricity, machinery that can cover such a large size bomb, launchers, launching pads, and tracts of six metres length. This was -- this could not be made in Sarajevo so there were a series of reasons. I could give you an endless list of such reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As I heard a moment ago from you, when answering questions from the Prosecution, that the fuse factory was in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And that was under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Croatia. So fuses were available?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What is the point of a fuse if you don't have a projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you're categorical in stating that no one else at the beginning of the conflict had these air bombs except the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. The HOV had them, too, in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Wasn't it possible, then, at a certain period of time, especially in 1995 when the HOV was together with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina creating one army, such air bombs, or even rocket bombs or launchers, could be obtained from the army belonging to the HOV?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How are you going to transport a launcher through the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We have been listening about this, but I can ask you directly. Through the tunnel everything could be transported through the tunnel that could be divided into parts and then assembled again?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Colleague Tapuskovic, hypothetically, everything is possible. The Americans could have provided rockets and everything in Sarajevo. They could have targeted those targets, instead of the army of Republika Srpska. If we're talking hypothetically, everything is possible. What I'm saying is the concept. If you have a rocket and you have a launcher, you have to have ten charts; and to be able to hit a target, you have to do some testing. As we are talking about air fuel, I told you earlier on in my earlier testimony that -- that only our colleagues from Vinca had fuel air, and they got them from the Americans in the mid-1980s. In Pretis, only the body was manufactured. In 1992, further development of aerosol fuel-air bombs was discontinued, and the manufacture transferred to Belgrade. And even if have you a bomb and you have rockets which you can purchase from the Serbia and Croats, as you say, and if you a launcher that somehow got to Sarajevo, you don't have the air fuel, the fuel air. You can't make it up, if you understand what I'm saying. And let me also say that the directions of fire show if you take a vehicle, which is quite large and can be seen on a flat area, if it is close to the line of conflict, that vehicle will be destroyed very quickly. And if we look at the structure of the soil where the incidents occurred and where that vehicle may have been deployed, it always had to be at least one kilometre away from the confrontation line and sheltered behind a building, so as not to be noticed or destroyed by mortar fire or heavy artillery. So the system is highly complex. If you look at Sarajevo, the configuration of the land, it is very elongated. Therefore, if a vehicle were to move through Sarajevo of such large size with a rocket that was not noticed by military observers or the citizens or the counter-intelligence, the counter-intelligence and the intelligence service never said that it had identified such weapons during 1992. And everything could be seen because Sarajevo is in a valley, and the observation forces were on a higher altitude. Therefore, I cannot accept this thesis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shorter answers in future.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Even at night-time?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In all these incidents, there were only two incidents that took place at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I was thinking -- I wasn't thinking of the time of the incident, but the time when one had to pass unnoticed through Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You can't launch anything unnoticed in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could the witness be shown document DD00-1724, and there's a translation by the translation service of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see this order, please? As you were working with explosives, when there is reference made to the 3rd of November, 1994, to all the corps, an order is issued. "Recently commands in units in depots and in work areas, there have been lapses in the protection and handling of lethal weapons, of ordnance with the gravest consequence, loss of life." And then comes the order: "Immediately approach the storing and protection of UBS, in the spirit of the instructions and prescribed technical norms and criteria, and give thorough training to personnel who handle these materials, especially UBS filled with D1 explosives guarded in secure places." As you were working with explosives, which you collected in the way that you have just explained, is it right to say that the army Bosnia and Herzegovina, independently of that, had explosives that it used for the manufacture of weapons that is referred to here?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me say immediately that I was active in 1992/1993. This document is dated from the end of 1994. Explosive D1 is an explosive manufactured in Tuzla, a surrogate of a real explosive, if I may describe it in that way, and which had a lot of negative characteristics when it came to handling, sensitivity to external parameters. That is why this order was issued. Its effectiveness was poor; two or three times poorer than TNT. This was an attempt because in 1994 there was still problems with the supply of explosives to reach the territory under the army's control, and this was an attempt to find some alternative source. If I may explain what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you can confirm that such explosives were available?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D174, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Talking about air bombs, you spoke about their shortcomings, the risks. You know that a number of these bombs that we are talking about here were unexploded?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If there were any such unexploded bombs, could they have also been used to produce an air bomb within Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you, in order to melt the explosive, you would have to heat the whole projectile. For me to be able to bring a 200-kilometre [as interpreted] bomb, I would have to have a furnace with steam, a cauldron of a very large size. I would need to have a crane to raise the bomb, to separate the fuse, and then to try and melt the explosive in that cauldron in order to be able to reuse it. So this is an impossible mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But do come back to your expert report. Can we say that before that, in view of everything that we have heard, because of these activities you were involved with the manufacture weapons, because of your activities in manufacturing weapons in cooperation with the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that you are not an uninterested party, that you are directly interested in the problems that existed during the conflict, and therefore you are not totally impartial?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't agree. If I had been partial, I would be a general in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or I would be in the Ministry of Defence and not at the Mechanical Engineering Faculty. If I look at my biography, you will see that I had very firms principles, and you can consult your colleagues in Belgrade or Sarajevo or anywhere. I am a man of integrity. And what I believe, I say. You must admit that that is something that is not desirable in the Balkans, and you see, in 1993, I was replaced. I was dismissed because I didn't agree to certain things. After that, I never obtained any kind of position. I am working as a university teacher at the Faculty of Mechanical Engineering.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As you said, some of these air bombs that are mentioned here, and that you are specialising in, fell close to your house, and you were directly in jeopardy. You could have been a victim?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was a victim for four years, so it's rather ridiculous to focus on one particular day. I was interested in the phenomenon of what is being used, how it was being used. As for me, my family, my wife and children, we were exposed on a daily basis. Sometimes we were lucky that there was no shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but that is why I think as an expert you cannot be impartial.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, on the contrary. I think I can be impartial to a greater degree than most, because rarely will you come upon a situation that a man is four years exposed to artillery and mortar and rocket systems, that this same man worked on the production of such ammunition, and at the same time this person is trying to be a researcher. For me, this was a perfect experience to see the vast differences between theoretical approaches to certain ammunition, the tactics of their use, and their actual after effects. So I am a highly qualified person, and you will in not a single of my reports do -- do I provide my comments only, but I refer to British and American experts. So every conclusion or statement that I make is corroborated with physical and mathematics interpretations of incidents, not my subjective experience of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But not only that, Mr. Zecevic, you visited almost each of those sites - and I will come back to that later - when these things happened, and you spoke to witnesses, as you yourself say.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Not every event, but only a certain number of incidents that I was aware of and which I could reach.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Doesn't that also, in a certain sense, prevent you from being absolutely objective and professional in observing all these things that were happening? I think this prevents you from being an objective observer of the facts.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think you are wrong. Can you imagine a person who would now, 12 years later after the events, and who was not in Sarajevo and who was not working in the military industry, who did not rely only on investigators' reports. I had the possibility of monitoring the situation in 1994 and 1995, of motivating myself to investigate what was being done in the area in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the 22nd paragraph of your report; page 159 of the B/C/S and in English 180, page 180. The general context for the use of air bombs in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's the paragraph that tell us when exactly such bombs began to be used, who used them, and where the weapons were procured. In this first chapter, you say that the first incident you ever heard of was on the 29th of January, 1994 at 0945 hours. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In paragraph 3, you say that you heard in a television programme a statement of Karadzic's when he spoke of a "secret weapon" that had been supplied to his army, and you say that it was supposed to be a weapon that would turn around the whole war. It's not written here exactly but --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Don't put that sentence in my mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I read it somewhere. I'll find it later. At any rate, can we say that it was a weapon that could, indeed, have turned the war around, in view of all its characteristics?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The results of a conflict are based on manpower, technology superiority, and psychological effects. If panic occurs, then these weapons become questionable, and that's why that weapon had an extreme effect on people, such as disorganisation. Can you imagine a person sitting in their apartment when a projectile hits and just blows off the -- the top three floors of a building of a sky-scraper? It's intimidating. Can you imagine that situation when the sky-scraper was hit. From their psychological point of view, it was indeed a formidable effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would it have been possible for the BH army to achieve that effect by pursuing such propaganda?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the main task of the propaganda was to diminish the panic, not to cause it, not to spread it. My answer to the question would be negative, because the purpose of every army is to mobilise its people, its troops, and to raise the morale, rather than destroy their own population because panic and disorganisation can only result from that. Everybody starts avoiding the army. I don't think that argument holds water.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think you understood me. You were talking about the psychological effect of such a thing on the population of Sarajevo and the troops in Sarajevo, the troops that were in the city. I'm asking you precisely about that. If the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had been able to resort to such activities, especially in those cases where there were no victims, no casualties, and there were just a few such cases, just to achieve the psychological effect while blaming the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you, again. The specifications of modified bombs, such as FAB-250 that had to be launch from a vehicle, from a distance of several kilometres, are uncontrollable. So you cannot reckon with hitting a particular building without causing casualties. We have already discussed this. There is no army that can control the flight of such a projectile and have it hit a particular building, unless it is a guided missile; therefore, that was not possible. It couldn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have one document, and I must say that I'm in two minds, whether to present it or not, or whether to produce it now or later. It's DD00-1830. I will produce it now. A translation is supplied. It's by a court-sworn translator from Belgrade. And when this document is shown to the witness, we'll see that it's a signed document. Let's move to page 3. We see that it's signed army General Rasim Delic. If the Court decides to admit this document, the Trial Chamber will have occasion to read it but also the witness. You will see that the document speaks of possible panic that may result, and also the document does not state there was a single human victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But what I want to put to you, Witness, is this. In the order, that we can see on page 2, it reads under paragraph 1. The order is dated 4th July, 1995, six days after that hit on the television building. And it says in paragraph 1: "I hereby order the intelligence administration, in cooperation with the President of the state committee for cooperation with UNPROFOR, shall take required activities with UNPROFOR regarding acquainting the international community with the mass and non-selective use of these devices." And in the last paragraph, before the signature, we read: "The commands of the units, whereever the lay of the land allows, shall select locations at Mojmilo, Igman, Vojkavica, Sokolje, and others for a similar response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the question? What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the first question is:

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did the witness know anything about this at the time when this order existed, because it was the time when he was investigating the incident of the 28th of August, following orders of the investigating judge, as he said himself.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I must have this document before me, because I don't see anything on the screen, in order to be able to -- to understand the gist of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why is not on the screen? It was on our screen in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, yes. Yes. Now, we can see this order quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think the witness wants to see it in his language. I'm a little confused. And maybe if he could be directed to a particular part of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's there now in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the order and item 1?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The intelligence administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see the last page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm waiting for the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't put this question otherwise than, did you know about this order?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. I was employed at the Faculty of Mechanical Engineering of the university, and I was engaged by a judge, who is a civilian person, to investigate the incident that occurred in the television building. This is an order from the commander of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, I cannot deal with this document any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But I would like to continue where we left off regarding the general context and your findings, paragraph 22. You see, after the reference to Karadzic's statement, you say: "I contacted the BH army Main Staff and following a discussion with General Arif Pasalic," which means right then on the 29th of January, 1994, "I sent him a brief report, and then set about drafting a paper on the characteristics of the fuel-air weapon. On completion, I sent it to the BH army Main Staff." So, again, in fact, this time you offered your own services to do this?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't. It's that I realised after seeing the remnants of the bomb that exploded close to my house on the 29th of January, I realised that it was a dangerous weapon; that is, of particular danger to the urban areas of Sarajevo. I wanted to acquaint the army, because in the BH army nobody knew anything about it, except me, perhaps, and two of my colleagues who are worked earlier in Pretis. I was a citizen of my country, and I thought that was what I should do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how else to put this, but doesn't that really discredit you as an expert witness, because from the word go you were directly interested. You were an interested party. You were partial. You were doing what you were doing in the interests of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I was working in the best interests of the citizens of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You have to wait for my question to finish.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would put this way: If you saw a fire in your neighbourhood, your first logical step, as a loyal citizen, was to pick up the receiver and call the fire brigade. I was a citizen of Sarajevo, a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I noted something that was of interest to anyone and everyone who was living in Sarajevo. My job, as a university lecturer, was to provide a intellectual contribution. I wrote a paper about it. If it is forbidden to think, and if it is forbidden to pass on any information that is available and that could help reduce the number of victims and casualties, then so be it. But I thought it was my right and duty as a human being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I did proceed from agreeing with you that it is a proper attitude. But while fulfilling your obligation as a human being towards the citizens and the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I still think that you brought yourself in a situation where you cannot speak here as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think this question has now been asked an answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. I think you're now arguing with the witness, Mr. Tapuskovic. The point has been made, and it's for the Chamber to make of it what we will.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is always up to the Trial Chamber to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, then you were invited by Judge Ismet Bazdarevic - and that is a passage just below the one that I read - and you invited, in your, turn two of your colleagues. Within ten days after the 28th of June, you made your paper as experts.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What are you trying to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you engaged in this work only from the moment when the explosion occurred, the one that caused damage?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have said this two or three times before. Yes, the judge summoned me and issued a formal decision engaging me as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now go back to your statement given on the 26th of February, 1996, DD00-1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Tapuskovic. Was the import of your question that the witness produced his report in a period of ten days?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says that within ten days, we collected a certain amount of information and compiled our expert report that we sent to -- submitted to Judge Bazdarevic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's correct, and it is written in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: While we're discussing this, why isn't that report attached? Why hasn't it been submit the together with your report.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't see why I should have been the one to submit it. I made it for the court. The court did not accept it. In that report -- in fact, I gave a copy of that report to the Prosecution in 1996. This time, I received specific questions from the OTP and I answered those questions. You may have noticed in the incident regarding the television building, I provided the results, the findings, of my investigations, and I built that into my comments. In every case, I distinguished between what the investigators said and what I was stating.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It's symptomatic, and I think requires explanation why that report is missing, the one that you submitted to the investigating judge, like the reports that others provided to you are provided?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I did my expert report for this occasion, and there are no deviations, no discrepancies, expect perhaps concerning minor details regarding the specifications of projectiles. It's not my responsibility whether the investigating judge will accept my report and whether she will send it on to The Hague or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a document here that I got from Alex Whiting, my learned friend of the Prosecution, an interview with the witness on the 19th of April, and it ends by saying, in relation to the interview that Mr. Whiting already mentioned here: "The Assistant Minister of Defence heard and did not react to those threats addressed by the MUP."

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Not the MUP, but the intelligence and counterintelligence officers from the Main Staff. Not the MUP, the not the MUP. I never had any problems with the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you say: "Professor Zecevic explained that a bomb with rocket motors actually has more destructive capacity than a TNT one, but that did not stop the pressure. He did not change his report, and then his report was not sent to The Hague with the others."

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is my impression. Why my report was not included in the official government reports. I really don't know who sends these reports to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, please speak into the microphone, perhaps come a little closer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I would just note that counsel, perhaps by misspeaking, misquoted the document that he is reading. It doesn't say that a bomb with rockets has more destructive capacity. It says that a fuel-air bomb has more destructive capacity than a TNT bomb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now move on to the statement that you made on the 26th and 27th. Here is page 1. Is that the statement that you gave? A few moments ago, you said yes.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at page 4. In English it is page 4, paragraph 6, and you say here, as far as air bombs are concerned, you talk about them. You say: "I made my own conclusions about air bombs," and then you say who used them. You mention the Russians and the Vietnamese and -- the U.S. in Vietnam, rather; by the Russians in Afghanistan, by the Israelis in the near East; so not only the Russians. These bombs that are mentioned here were used by the Americans, Russians in Afghanistan, and the Israelis in the near East, as you put it here.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Look, air bombs, not modified rocketised bombs. That is the only difference. It was only the Russians who had would carried out this modification of an air bomb with rocket motors. Americans dropped fuel air bombs from planes, and the Israelis created a special rocket system that launched the projectiles with fuel-air explosives, but it was not a modification. A completely new system was developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You just made one distinction here, if we go on reading this. These projectiles have a blast effect. These projectiles that you're talking about; Russians, American, Israelis; whereas, modified air bombs also cause a fragmentation effect. That is the only different that you say. You did not mention rocket propelled.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We are talking about effects here. Effects. I was interested in the effects.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, you say: "On the 27th of January 1994, at about 2:00, I heard a terrible explosion." Can you explain this? You say that it was on the 27th of January at 9:45, and now here you say here that the time when you gave this statement is closer to the actual time when this happened in February, 1996, I mean. So you say that it was on the 27th of January and around 2.00. What is correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth at that time, in 1994, my computer said 9:45; whereas, this is an interview I had with the Prosecutor two years later. And, quite simply, that's what I told him, around 1400 hours. This absolutely plays no role. Whether it's 9.00 or 2.00, it is a matter of virtual time that one feels in moments like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Observe a pause between question and answer in the interests of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since your report is not in the electronic system, you have it in front of you, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes .

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 22.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please give me a page reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The page is 180 in English and 159 in B/C/S. "In the spring of 1995, people in the Novi Grad and Novo Sarajevo informed me that very powerful and high impact projectiles were being used. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now please look at your statement on page 5, B/C/S, and, in English, it is page 5, paragraph 2, in the middle. A sentence starts by the words: "In June 1995."

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And so, does that really change anything? I stand by my statements. I'm telling you yet again. I have documents where I recorded this. I have my own diary, my own agenda. This is a statement that I made two years after the actual event. There is no difference in content. It's just a matter of whether it was in April or June. It really has no effect on the importance of my claims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We have to leave that to the Court, I believe, the difference is considerable. But at any rate there is a difference, right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, look. When does summer start? May I ask you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. You may not. It is for counsel to ask questions. Now let us move on, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please look at what it says after that, that in June six or seven projectiles were fired from Lukavica, Vojkovici from the area called Pavlovac. None of these projectiles hit the TV building. All of them landed in front or behind the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So is it correct that at that time, in June, even six projectiles were fired at the TV building?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know whether that was the intention, to fire at the TV building. I only identified on the map the sites of impact and, when you look at these places, then it is rather indicative, if can I put it that way. But perhaps the target of these attacks was to actually hit the TV building. That is perhaps the context that you should look at this. Page 130, take a look. Red and white little circles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: These are six or seven projectiles that are referred to here. But in the next paragraph, and that's why I'm asking all of this, starts with the following words in the second sentence: "I investigated these impacts unofficially." And then you visited the wire factory and then some other buildings; that is to say, before the TV building was hit, yet again you unofficially investigated all these impacts that occurred before the 28th. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Where does this -- where -- where does it say that, "unofficially."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the second paragraph -- rather, in the same paragraph, in the second sentence. The beginning of the third paragraph, B/C/S, and in English, the fifth paragraph -- or rather, in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I can be of assistance I think the witness is looking at his report whereas counsel is talking about his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I beg your pardon. Not your report. Your statement. Please take a look at your statement, and it says here: "Rumours were that there -- these were modified air bombs." You see that.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you go on to say I investigated these impacts unofficially, and then you visited the wire factory and all these other places. You describe all of that. So before the investigative judge asked you to do so, you actually carried out your own investigation.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, I didn't say investigation. I looked into it. I already said two or three times that I wanted to understand the phenomenology of what was going on. I wanted to be familiarised with this. I did not carry out an investigation. I just went to the actual site to see what had happened. I did not have an objective that is required by an investigation. I just needed to have this information. What happened. Whether it could jeopardise my safety, the safety of my family, of other people, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you now please look at page 7. Page 7. Not your expert report; the statement. In English it is page 7, paragraph 5, and then the end of this long paragraph the sentence reads as follows: "It is the first time that --" we're talking about these bombs. "They were first used in June 1993 when they hit objects in town. One motor had a marking, one --" so on and so forth. This last part meant that the motor was produced in 1993. They obviously were not able to apply a parachute to the projectile so they adapted a Russian projectile to their own launch system. The motors were not properly attached to the body and the stabilisers were fixed in an amateur way, so it was obvious that they did not care where it would fall. You see? You say this was first used in the month of June 1993 when they hit objects in town?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that you have read this right. What I said here was this was the first time that rocket motors of 122-millimetres were used in Sarajevo, that were modified in Sarajevo, so there was this ring that was put on the projectile. The external diameter was 122 millimetres -- 128 millimetres and the internal one was 122 for it to be able to be launched from Oganj, which is of 128-millimetre calibre. That's what it says here. So we can conclude these were Russian motors that were imported by Serbia, and in Serbia they had external rings of 128 millimetres so they could be launched from the launchers that the army of Republika Srpska had and that on them there was this marking. I'm sorry. I mean, yes, well, I agree I am speaking too fast and I'm really sorry about that. I will try to slow down. 122 is what it says here, and then 128. M 91, 9301. And that shows that this rocket motor had been adapt in the year of 1993, in the first month of the year of 1993. And that in 1993 it was the motor not the fuel-air bomb was -- just read on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
