utterances.text: All right. Let it be. Now I'd like to go back to your expert report, page 71 in English and 66 in B/C/S, where you speak of rocketised FAB-100 bombs.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So it pertains to the bombs that were referred to here. There is no doubt about that. And what it says here is: "On the basis of reports that came in during 1994 and 1995, it was observed that rocket-assisted FAB-100 and FAB-250 aircraft bombs were being used heavily both on the city of Sarajevo and on other parts of the front, Olovo, Bihac, Gorazde, Postalina, Doboj, Tesanj, Tuzla, et cetera. So can we say that these FAB-100 and FAB-250 bombs were used throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina and that it was not the first time that they -- well, sort of fell and -- fell in Sarajevo, hit Sarajevo in June 1995?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I just mentioned here that there was this piece of information, and this information came through the information media, the mass media, and I said so very clearly. On the basis of information coming in, but, no, no, no doubt that this existed in other fronts. And I also quoted the army of Republika Srpska here in my analysis, and you can see that the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, and there are copies of telexes in the Slobodan Milosevic case where an order of the Main Staff is being referred to addressed to the director of the Pretis factory, stating how many rocket launchers should be placed, where and how many bombs and where these bombs should be sent, and in these documents of the Main Staff of the army Republika Srpska, there is mention of Doboj, Teslic and Sarajevo and a few other locations. So there this is other document, SHS and SBS, and in English ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: About that as it may, whoever was firing those projectiles one may say with certainty that they did not appear for the first time in the spring of 1995 but that this was something that was present in those conflicts throughout and in the way you have just described?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me finally go back once again to your statement of the 26th and 27th of February, DD00-1985 -- 87. Of the B/C/S, and of the English the last paragraph of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But before that -- or shall we deal with this first. Just look at the last paragraph in the B/C/S and in the English. You say, and I quote: "Technically this projectile was not perfect. In my opinion, it was made by people not fully familiar with adapting weapons, but it was a good idea from the military point of view." In what sense? Could you explain that to the Judges, please.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's very simple. These weapons, if they were to be used according to certain established principles where troops are concentrated as you were able to see in the order of General Delic when he speaks about the attack by tank units from Lukavica as a possibility, if such projectiles were to be used, it can cause a drop in morale of the troops. So in 1994, January, the first projectile that was launched was directed towards the front lines and not the built-up parts of the town. Later on, this changed. And I'm saying that if two or three such rockets or two or three launchers, or two launchers with two rockets each, if they had been launched towards a point where there was a concentration of the resistance on the part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, those peoples' morale would have dropped very quickly, and the army of Republika Srpska would have made a breakthrough very quickly. Why they didn't use this, I don't know. Weapons were irrationally used in Sarajevo from the military standpoint, not to kill civilians but from the military standpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to that when we study each of your reports about individual incidents. The last sentence says: "Our authorities did not" -- this is the last sentence of this statement. "... did not appreciate that these weapons are unsuited for use against military targets and are only effective as indiscriminate weapons against civilian population." In other words, is this true, too, your assessment that this shouldn't be used, but does that mean that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had such weapons but they didn't want to use them?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, you didn't get the point. What I said here was that technically this projectile was not perfect and because in Sarajevo one by one projectile was launched not in a burst of fire, but several projectiles within a small period of time, and this -- the effect of such projectiles was not very great from the military standpoint. However, its effect on built-up areas of Sarajevo, individual effect, led to disorientation of the population, led to panic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe the point which Mr. Tapuskovic is making is that the words "our authorities" would appear to refer to the authorities both of the -- the RSA and the ABiH. And that is why he wants to know whether, in suggesting that the ABiH authorities did not appreciate that the weapons could be used indiscriminately, you're not implying that they also had those weapons. So I think it's the words "our authorities" which require some clarification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that point in time, for me, there was only one authority, and that was the authority of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it was only at the end of 1996 that the present concept was constituted as a result of the application of the Dayton Accords. And I was -- I pointed this out when making the statement, I was referring to the period up to 1995, not after 1995, because it was no longer important. Fighting stopped. Peace was re-established and so on. When I say "our authorities," I'm implying the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the period from 1994/1995, from 1992, 1994, 1995. I'm quite precise in that respect. Because, if I may have noticed, my expert report about air fuel bombs for the Court was not adopted. I had some unpleasantness with officers of the Main Staff who came to persuade me to change it, instead of putting air fuel that I should put TNT. I didn't agree to that, because they didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, a moment ago you mentioned the name of Slobodan Milosevic. In the Milosevic case, you were a witness?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the honest truth, I don't remember. I testified four or five times so far.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness approach the microphone.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Says the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As you are an expert in this case, I would like to show you the last paragraph of your interview with Mr. Chester Stamp, DD00-2035. Last page; English page 6, paragraph 3. We see the end of this statement, rather, of this conversation: "Professor Zecevic handed the team a photocopied report by a Serbian mortar expert scientist, Miroljub Vukasinovic, concerning his findings about the mortar attack of Markale market in August 1995. Professor Zecevic stated that whilst of course the incidents are separate, the information contained within the report is of relevance to the February the 5th, 1994 incident." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that that report which you received and handed at the time to the investigators of the OTP relates to the event of the 28th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is what is said here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I should now like to show you that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DD00-2007. There's an English translation at the end of that document, DD-2007. DD00-2007. And before the bibliography that the Professor relies on. We have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "Conclusion: On the basis of the analysis of the crater and geometry of stabiliser, as well as numerical simulations of the explosion of the projectile on the target, it can be claimed that the shell explosion was most probably carried out in static conditions at an angle between 50 and 60 degrees. For these values of the angle of descent, if the shell had been fired from Serbian positions, it would have definitely activated on the roof of the building." Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to -- I'm going to object because I don't -- this is -- this is a report -- this is an article written by somebody else about an incident that the witness has not testified about. So I'm not sure what the relevance is -- I'm not sure how he could possibly comment on this, on somebody else's report, on something that he has not himself testified about. It seems like a strange time to bring this into the examination. I just don't see how he -- how this witness can comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we are past the time to -- for the break. In my view, the witness should be allowed to answer the question: Do you remember this? And then we'll see whether he knows anything about the contents of the document. But we're going to break now and please note where we're at. It's 5.00. It's five past 5.00. I see you are looking puzzled. We break at 5.00 on Friday. Do you wish to work until 7.00, Mr. Tapuskovic? Because in that event, perhaps separate arrangements can be made for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that you don't have to do anything special for me. Allow me only to examine the witness for as long as you have ruled I would have. I have hardly used half of that time. Maybe it is a little late.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're breaking for the -- for the weekend and we resume. You will resume your cross-examination Monday morning at 9.00. So we stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 23rd day of April, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
